threads.subject: Passport related matters for visa application -- REP-2020-2315
threads.question:
Good day,
Yes, it is possible to request a replacement TRV counterfoil be affixed to a client's new passport so long as it is still valid. A replacement counterfoil would be issued to the original validity of the document. If the foreign national would prefer a TRV with a different validity, they would need to submit a new application and pay the associated fees.
In order to request a replacement counterfoil, clients can submit a web form request indicating the type of enquiry
(Replacement Documents, Amendments to documents and Verification of status documents) and simply provide the
supporting rationale and both the residential address and mailing address in the 'Your enquiry' field. Once the appropriate office receives the request, they will send the client instructions on how to pay the $30 and where to submit their original passport and self-addressed stamped (traceable means only) envelope.
If the information about the client's place of birth was not communicated in their original TRV application, they would not be eligible for a replacement TRV; they will need to submit a new application given information was not part of the original assessment of the client's application.
We do recommend the client get a new passport with the correct place of birth as it would help avoid any complications when applying as well as when travelling.
Otherwise, we recommend that the client, upon applying for a new TRV, note their correct place of birth on their application, present an explanation of their situation, proof that they are in the process of applying for a new passport with the correct information (if applicable), and that they submit a certified copy of their birth certificate as a supporting document.
Please note that failure to present this information would constitute misrepresentation and may lead to a 5 year exclusion order.
If they do travel with the passport with the incorrect place of birth, we also recommend that they carry a certified copy of their birth certificate with them when they travel as supporting evidence to avoid the possibility of being found inadmissible for misrepresentation.
I hope this provides some clarity.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: NOC Code under Express Entry -- REP-2020-2700
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: One of my Clients worked for a company for about 290 days in Canada, and then he lost his job due to COVID-19. In order to complete one (1) year full-time Canadian work experience to be eligible to claim Canadian work experience points under Express Entry, should his NOC code under the new job be the same as his previous NOC?
Answer: To apply for the Canadian Experience Class the applicant must have accumulated 12 months of full-time Canadian skill work experience (or the equivalent in part-time work) in one or more Noc 0,A, or B occupations within the 36 months before the date of application receipt, as per R87.1(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. The officer must be satisfied that the applicant performed the actions described in the lead statement of the occupational description of the NOC, and the applicant must have performed a substantial number of main duties, including all the essential duties as per the NOC. Please see our website for more information.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Change of Primary NOC in Express entry after ITA -- REP-2020-2715
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: I am writing to you in regards to Express Entry, both FSW as well as CEC class. Is it possible to change the NOC after receiving ITA in either of the streams? I do understand that for FSW the CLB requirements for NOC 0, A and B is CLB 7 and for CEC class CLB requirement for NOC 0, A is CLB 7, whereas for NOC B is CLB 5. Other than the requirement of remaining eligible after ITA as well, is it possible to change the NOC of work experience or primary NOC?
E.g., sometimes the applicant accidentally chooses NOC 2173 however when he receives the job reference letter the job duties best match NOC 2714. Is it possible to make such minor changes in NOC after receiving ITA or will the visa officer refuse the application. Answer: Express Entry candidates are responsible for ensuring that the information in their profile is accurate and up-to-date at all times. Candidates are assessed on whether or not they meet to requirements of the program based on the information provided in their expression of interest. In order to be assigned points for Canadian work experience, the applicant must specify in their expression of interest the four-digit in the NOC that corresponds with the work they’ve engaged in, as per 15(4)(a) of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system. While it's entirely possible that the applicant has made an error when applying and should have applied under a different NOC, the applicant was issued an ITA based on the information provided under the expression of interest and submitted their e-APR based on this information. The officer assessing the application must be satisfied that the applicant continues to qualify for the program they’ve applied for based on the NOC code mentioned in the expression of interest. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements. We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Completing an e-APR with an expired U.S. passport -- REP-2020-2767
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: Our client received an ITA for Express Entry. At the time he submitted his Express Entry profile, his U.S. passport was valid. Our client's passport has since expired. He has applied for a new U.S. passport using an expedited U.S. process but has been advised by the U.S. government that his passport will not be issued to him until after his ITA expires. If the answer to #1 is "yes", should he use the process for expired passports (i.e. add 5 years to the expiry date in the e-APR and include a letter of explanation that includes the correspondence from the U.S. passport office as to the delay).
Answer: Yes, the applicant can submit their e-APR with an expired passport, however the applicant must have a valid passport to come to Canada. Upon submission of the e-APR, please include a Letter of Explanation which confirms that the applicant is in the process of obtaining a new passport. Please provide a copy of the new passport as soon as it's received. Our website has instructions as to how to update an application which is already in progress. The instructions in your second question are for passport holders only, please follow the instructions linked above for providing IRCC a copy of the new passport.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Adding non-accompanying spouse after e-APR in Express Entry -- REP-2020-2774
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: Can a principal applicant make his non-accompanying spouse (currently staying with PA in Canada on a temporary status) as now accompanying after e-APR under Express Entry? Will this cause recalculation of CRS points? Is this practice valid to gain more CRS points?
Answer: Yes, family members can be added to the application at any time during the process, but must be added prior to obtaining permanent resident status. All family members must be examined as part of the electronic application for permanent residence, whether they are accompanying the principal applicant or not. The differing points grid in Express Entry was developed to reflect the increased economic success in Canada seen where the principal applicant has a spouse possessing certain competencies. IRCC does not support the use of these provisions in any kind of “strategic" way. We recommend that spouses who intend to live together in Canada, state that in their applications. Changing the partner's status from “non-accompanying" to “accompanying" during the processing of an application, up to the time of landing, may not constitute misrepresentation; however, this choice was never intended to be used as a strategy. Rather, it allows families to accurately describe their situation and intentions and to comply with section 16 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act on the obligation to answer truthfully. Therefore, the principal applicant's Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score will be recalculated to account for the change in situation, at all points in the process.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

How the COVID-19 program delivery for work permits applies to C-11 work permits I am having difficulty reconciling IRCC's Work permit: COVID-19 program delivery with outside of Canada C-11 work permit applicants (persons applying for a LMIA exempt work permit (exemption code C-11) as a self-employed applicant under R205(a)). Yes, C11 work permit applicants may be exempt from the travel restrictions if they have been issued a letter of introduction for a valid job offer. However, the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) makes the final determination on entry to Canada. Guidance provided by the CBSA for entrepreneurs/self-employed persons:
While the client meets one of the following exemption: 3(1)(m) a person whose application for a work permit referred to in paragraph (I) was approved under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and who has received written notice of the approval but who has not yet been issued the permit
The client still needs to demonstrate that their travel is non-discretionary. While, in general, work is consider non-discretionary, if the business is not operating, the travel will be considered discretionary. The Border Services Officer or Liaison Officer will verify with the client if the business is operating or not, and determine if the travel is non-discretionary.

Satisfying the valid job offer requirement Assuming that the answer to part 1 is "yes", would the temporary worker simply meet the "hold a valid job offer" requirement by writing a letter on their self-employed company's letterhead in which they explain that they are both the employer and the temporary worker and that they are coming to Canada to commence their self-employed activities? Yes, the employer and employee may be the same person in your scenario. In order for a work permit to be issued under the International Mobility Program, an offer of employment must be submitted using the Employer Portal. Due to COVID-19, you may be eligible to apply for a one-time open work permit of up to 18 months if you apply online by July
Permanent residence applicants can apply for the open work permit under the new public policy, if they meet the essential eligibility requirements.
To be eligible for this open work permit, you must meet the following 5 requirements:
1. Your post-graduation work permit (PGWP)
a. expired on or after January 30, 2020, or
b. will expire within 4 months from the date you apply for this open work permit.
2. You were in Canada as of January 27, 2021, when the public policy took effect, and have stayed in Canada since then.
3. You either
a. have a temporary resident status (this could be from having a valid PGWP, visitor record, or another permit that allows you to stay in Canada), or
b. lost your temporary resident status, but you’ve already applied to restore it, or
c. lost your temporary resident status, but you'll apply to restore it at the same time as applying for this open work permit
4. You include in your application that you’re applying for an open work permit under this public policy.
5. You have a valid passport.
a. The work permit will be issued for up to 18 months from the date of approval or until your passport expires, whichever comes first. For example, if your passport is valid for 6 months, then you will be issued an open work permit for 6 months.
b. To maximize the duration of the open work permit, make sure your passport is valid for at least 18 months from the date of approval.

Question: I would like to confirm that it is possible to add a spouse or common-law dependent to a Permanent Residency application in Express Entry that is already in process, without negative consequences. I understand that it is possible to add this dependent regardless of the impact in the main applicant's score in Express Entry. For example, somebody has a score of 460, receives an ITA with a 460 cut-off required, and submits her PR application. Answer: Yes, family members can be added to the application at any time during the process, but must be added prior to obtaining permanent resident status. All family members must be examined as part of the electronic application for permanent residence, whether they are accompanying the principal applicant or not. Applicants are instructed to inform IRCC of any changes to their family composition. If your situation changes, you should re-calculate your score before applying online for permanent residence. If your re-calculated score is less than the lowest score in your round of invitations, you should decline the invitation. Section A11.2 does not apply when an applicant adds a family member to their application after the submission of their electronic application for permanent residence; however, the family member will still have to be assessed, and pay the fees online.

while they are waiting for a decision on their post-graduation work permit application].

threads.answer:
Good day,
Apologies for the delay, this is in response to your enquiry regarding the eligibility to work under R186(w).
The authorization to work under R186(w) only applies to students who applied for their work permit prior to their study permit expiry date. Graduates who applied for a PGWP while under implied status are not eligible to work while waiting for a decision on their PGWP.
Furthermore, students who complete their program of study but aren't ready to apply for a PGWP right away must change their status to visitor if they want to remain in Canada, since they no longer meet the requirements of the student class. Since 2019, graduates no longer need to have a valid study permit in order to apply for a PGWP.
Please note that until further notice, as a temporary facilitative measure, students can apply for their PGWP before receiving their letter of completion and final transcripts. These documents will be requested when the processing officer assesses the application. This measure allows more students to apply for their PGWP when their study permit is still valid, and be eligible to work without a work permit under R186(w).

threads.question:
Dear Sir or Madam,
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
I am a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant registered under
I would like to have your clarification for the following:
The Express Entry system calculates the points for work experience based on months. For example, if a person started working on Jan 31 2020, when it's December 1, 2020, the system will calculate the points based on one year of work experience as the system will calculate points based on the period January to December (12 months). We know that the client would not have a year of work experience yet at that point yet.
When considering the Canadian Experience Class, if the client receives an invitation to apply in that condition, but completes that full 12 months by the time of the submission, would their application be accepted? Or should we wait for the full completion of one year to accept an invitation to apply?
Thank you for your clarification.

mmigration, Refugees Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
The Express Entry system calculates the points for work experience based on months. For example, if a person started working on Jan 31 2020, when it's December 1, 2020, the system will calculate the points based on one year of work experience as the system will calculate points based on the period January to December (12 months). We know that the client would not have a year of work experience yet at that point yet.
When considering the Canadian Experience Class, if the client receives an invitation to apply in that condition, but completes that full 12 months by the time of the submission, would their application be accepted? Or should we wait for the full completion of one year to accept an invitation to apply?
Answer:
The IRCC system calculates work experience by calculating months and not actual days worked in the month. IRCC is aware some applicants are receiving an ITA a month or two early and we advise the candidate not to delay their eAPR or turn down the invitation if the work experience is continuing. If the work genuinely ended before accumulating one year of work however, they should decline the invitation.
IRCC examining officers are aware of this, and when looking at the application they will take into consideration factors such as the continuous work status, the Offer of Employment Letter from the same employer, and whether the applicant reached the experience required by the time the application is processed.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

threads.question:
Bonjour,
La présente est en réponse à votre message du 27 janvier 2021.
Tel qu'indiqué sur le site web d'IRCC, les enfants mineurs qui souhaitent étudier au Canada doivent présenter une demande de permis d’études avant leur entrée au Canada. Ceci comprend les enfants mineurs qui sont accompagnés de leurs parents qui possèdent déjà un permis d’études ou de travail valide.
Si les enfants viennent au Canada en compagnie de leurs parents qui sont titulaires d’un permis d’études ou d’un permis de travail valide, ils n'ont pas besoin de fournir une lettre d’acceptation d'un établissement lorsqu'ils présentent une demande de permis d'études.
Un enfant mineur d’un parent qui n’est pas autorisé à travailler ou à étudier au Canada (par exemple, un parent qui est au Canada à titre de visiteur) n’est pas admissible à étudier au Canada sans permis d’études. Ces enfants mineurs doivent demander un permis d’études à partir de leur pays de dernière résidence permanente.
Les permis d’études pour les élèves du primaire sont délivrés pour une période d’un an et peuvent être renouvelés, alors que les permis d’études délivrés aux élèves inscrits à une école secondaire (de la 9º à la 12º année dans toutes les provinces et tous les territoires à l’exception du Québec, et de la 9º à la 11º année au Québec) peuvent se voir délivrer un permis pour la durée totale prévue de leurs études dans une école secondaire du Canada (maximum de quatre ans).
Les enfants mineurs qui fréquentent la maternelle et les classes préscolaires ne sont pas tenus d’avoir un permis d’études valide.
Important : De manière générale, les personnes qui demandent un permis d’études, y compris celles qui étudient aux niveaux primaire et secondaire, doivent fournir une lettre d’acceptation de l’établissement d’enseignement en question au Canada. Les demandeurs peuvent fournir soit la lettre d’acceptation originale soit une lettre sur support électronique.
Il existe une exception à cette exigence : Les enfants mineurs qui accompagnent un membre de la famille qui a demandé un permis de travail ou un permis d’études avant d’entrer au Canada et se l’est vu accorder ne sont pas tenus de fournir une lettre d’acceptation d’un établissement d’enseignement.
Nous espérons que ces renseignements vous seront utiles.
Merci,
Représentants immigration (IRCC)

threads.subject: 12 month bar H&C applications, applicability to dependent children -- REP-2020-2766
threads.question:
Good day,
I have a client (principal applicant-PA), for whom I am in the process of putting together an H&C application. PA has two daughters, years old, who can be included in her application as dependent children who are presently in Canada.
PA just informed me that her ex-husband recently entered Canada and intends to file a refugee claim, with the assistance of another lawyer. PA's husband wants to include the two daughters in his refugee claim, given that they too were affected by the persecution he suffered (but not the PA, she was already separated from the ex-husband at the time of the events).
Can the daughters still be included in PA's H&C application, or must they choose between their mother's H&C and their father's refugee claim? I am obviously aware of the prohibition on submitting an H&C application while a refugee claim is in process and the 12 month bar following a negative refugee decision; but in this case, it is the dependent children, and not the PA, who would have a pending refugee claim. There is no guidance in the H&C operational bulletin. ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/permanent-residence/humanitarian-compassionate-consideration/intake-who-may-apply.htiml#refugee-claim)
Please advise. Thanks!
Page 1720
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Good day
In your query, you wish to know whether a person – specifically, your client's two daughters – may be included as a dependent in both a refugee claim and an H&C application at the same time. You note that, while it is clear from the Program Delivery Instructions (PDIs) that a principal applicant cannot submit an H&C application while a refugee claim is in process and for 12 months following, this is not as clear in the case of the dependent children.
Respons e
The bar on applying for H&C while a refugee claim is in process and for 12 months following applies equally to dependents as it does to the principal applicant. The daughters cannot be included in both the H&C application and the refugee claim at the same time and will have to choose between their mother's H&C application and their father's refugee claim.
Note that, if the daughters choose to not file a refugee claim at this time and their father receives a positive decision on his claim and goes on to file an application for permanent residence as a protected person, he may include the daughters in his application for permanent residence at that time provided that they still meet the definition of“family member" in R1(3).
Similarly, if the daughters choose not to be included in their mother's H&C application at this time, their mother may ask to have them added to the H&C application at any point before it is finalized provided the bar on H&C does not continue to apply to the
daughters and that they continue to meet the definition offamily member" in R1(3).
Background
A review of the exceptions to applying for H&C contained in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) under A25(1.2) (known as the H&C bar) reveals that this section does not distinguish between the principal claimant and/or applicant and their dependents. Instead, this section lays out the exceptions to applying H&C in reference to the foreign national, a status
that applies to both the principal applicant and their dependents. For example, the section states,
A25(1.2) The Minister may not examine the request if
(b) the foreign national has made a claim for refugee protection that is pending before the Refugee Protection Division or the Refugee Appeal Division
Thus, it is becomes clear that this section of the Act applies to both the principal applicant and any dependents who wish to request H&C consideration.
Furthermore, when filing a refugee claim as a family, it is important to note that, while the claims may be joined, each person is
distinguished as an individual in the IRB decision as all have technically made a claim for protection. In other words, a dependent is considered a claimant in their own right rather than just an extra element of the principal claimant's claim. Thus, if the children's father includes his two daughters in his refugee claim, besides the father, the two daughters will also be considered to have a pending refugee claim.
Bringing these two elements together, it becomes clear that, if the daughters were to be included in their father's refugee claim, they would fall under the description of foreign nationals who have made a claim for refugee protection that is pending before the Refugee Protection Division or the Refugee Appeal Division. Thus A25(1.2) would apply and the daughters would be barred from applying for H&C.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Changes to compensation due to fluctuations in exchange rate -- REP-2020-2857
threads.question:
Good day
Thank you for reaching out to us about salaries and benefits paid in foreign currencies. You will find below the answers to your questions.
I understand that an employer is responsible for providing a foreign worker with wages that are substantially the
same but not less favourable than those in the offer of employment.
That is correct.
In the case where an employer is providing wages or allowances to an foreign worker, and the amount of the wages or allowances are converted from a foreign currency to Canadian currency, would the employer continue to be compliant if the Canadian value of the allowances decreased as a result of fluctuations in the exchange rate between
the foreign currency and the Canadian currency?
When submitting a job offer, the employer will indicate the Canadian wage that will be paid to the foreign national. If this salary is paid in a foreign currency, it must be identified under the "alternative compensation scheme" section of the offer and the conversion of the foreign currency into Canadian currency will be added under the wage section of the offer. The conversion must be made only at the time of the offer and must not be modified even if the exchange rate of the two currencies changes.
For example, if the applicant was eligible for an international assignment allowance of USD$500 per month, and at the time of application the allowance was noted in the Offer of Employment as CAD$700 based on the exchange rate at the time, if 6 months into the assignment, the allowance decreases to CAD$650 due to fluctuations in the exchange rate, how would IRCC view this change? In this case, as long as it was determined under the "alternate compensation scheme" that the allowance was set at US$500 and at the time of reporting the conversion equaled to C$700, the employer will have to continue to pay the amount of US$500 without adjusting the exchange rate.
Would the employer still be considered compliant since the exchange rates are outside of their control? The employer will continue to pay the same amount in foreign currency as indicated in the offer.
The same question can be asked about fluctuations that occur due to changes in the EPF Statutory Rate that impact the amount of allowance a foreign worker receives. Would pre-emptively indicating in the Offer of Employment that the foreign worker's wages and allowances are subject to fluctuations in the exchange rate address any compliance issues that could arise from decreases or increases in the value of the wages or allowances caused by these fluctuations. The same would be true in this scenario, and the foreign currency indicated in the job offer should be the same and no less favorable even if the exchange rates between the two currencies change.
Please note that in all cases that the employer must comply with provincial labour legislations.
We trust you will find this information useful.

Regards,

threads.subject: ACQUIRED WORK EXPERIENCE IN QUEBEC-Home Child Care Provider Pilot and Home Support
threads.question:
Worker Pilot -- REP-2020-2718
Greetings,
Please accept our apologies for the delay in responding to your enquiry. You will find below the answers to your questions.
1. Can a Home Child Care Provider ( CNP 4411 OR 4412) who acquired her work experience- 24 months in the province of Quebec apply for PR under the Pilot and Home Support Worker Pilot ? Given that she genuinely has the intention to move outside Quebec. Actually her intention is that once she obtains her open work permit is to find a job in same category outside Quebec and fully move outside Quebec.
Based on the information provided, the question appears to be for a caregiver who acquired 24 months work experience in the province of Quebec, who intends to move outside of Quebec once she obtains her permanent residence. Only applicants who indicate on their Schedule 19a-Home Child Care Provider (HCCP) or Home Support Worker (HSW)- Education and Language Assessment [IMM 5982] that they have not yet completed at least 24 months experience are issued an occupation-restricted open work permit under the HCCP/HSW Pilots (TR-to-PR process). Those who indicate that they have already met the work experience requirement are not be issued this occupation-restricted work permit, though they could be eligible for a bridging open work permit (straight-to-PR process).
The work experience gained in the province of Quebec can count as qualifying experience for caregivers applying under the straight-to-PR process, provided it otherwise meets all other criteria. Please refer to the Program Delivery Instructions specific to the Qualifying Canadian work experience for more details on what constitutes eligible experience. Caregivers applying under the TR-to-PR process will receive an occupation-restricted open work permit that will have the following condition: "may not engage in employment in the province of Quebec".
To note, all officers assessing applications submitted under Federal economic immigration programs are required to assess the intent of the applicant to reside outside Quebec as a permanent resident, under terms of jurisdiction governing selection of economic immigrants outlined in the Canada-Quebec Accord. For this reason, immigrants applying under the federal Economic Class programs must intend to establish in Canada outside Quebec, and must satisfy an officer regarding that intent. Assessing the genuineness of intent to reside can be supported by a range of documents/information, including but not limited to the applicant's own declaration or affidavit of intent, job offers, rental agreements, home purchases or utility bills from outside of Quebec. It is up to the applicant to provide sufficient proof to satisfy the officer that they intend to reside outside of Quebec as a permanent resident.
2. when is the program re opening ? and what is the quota for 2021?
The HCCP and HSW Pilots' caps are counted per calendar year. Therefore, caps were reset to zero (and the HCCP Pilot reopened) on January 1st, 2021.
As indicated in IRCC's Help Centre answer to the question Is there a limit on the number of caregiver applications you accept under the pilots?, we process up to 5,500 applications each year under the caregiver pilots: •2,750 applications for the Home Child Care Provider Pilot •2,750 applications for the Home Support Worker Pilot

Spouses and common-law partners of post-graduation work permit holders, including the new public policy 18 month open work permit, may be eligible to apply for an open work permit under the C41 exemption for (spouses and common-law partners of skilled workers). A dependent spouse or common-law partner is eligible to apply for an open work permit under Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) exemption code C41 if the principal foreign worker
- holds a work permit that is valid for a period of at least 6 months, or, if working under the authority of section R186 without a work permit, presents evidence that they will be working for a minimum of 6 months;
- is employed in an occupation that falls within National Occupational Classification (NOC) skill type 0 (management occupations) or skill level A or B (which generally includes professional occupations and technical or skilled trades [see the NOC website]);
- physically resides or plans to physically reside in Canada while working.

threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: To meet the MEC under the Express Entry FSW category, one must have accumulated, over a continuous period, at least 1 year of paid, full-time work experience (or the equivalent in part time work) in their primary occupation that is skill type 0, A or B within the last 10 years.
It is well known that primary teachers work for 9-10 months of the year and then are off work for scheduled summer breaks. I believe that these scheduled summer breaks can make it difficult for teachers to prove the minimum 1 year continuous paid requirement to qualify for FSW.
Where an American teacher does not have a formal contract clearly stating the term of employment, would providing a letter from the school stating that he/she was employed on a year-round basis with scheduled breaks for the summer (or that his/her term of employment was considered 1 entire year) plus evidence of pay stubs issued continuously all year (including throughout the scheduled summer break) be sufficient to prove the 1 year continuous paid requirement to qualify for FSW?
Presumably the law was not written with the intent to automatically disqualify teachers from ever qualifying under FSW because of the fact that they have scheduled summer breaks.
Answer: To meet the minimum work experience criteria for the Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) program, the applicant must have accumulated at least one year of continuous full-time (or the equivalent in part-time) paid work experience in a skilled occupation listed in Skill Type O, or Skill Level A or B of the National Occupational Classification (NOC), as per R75(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. To answer your question, if a teacher is able to demonstrate that they are a permanent full-time teacher, where summer and winter breaks were considered paid vacation with full pay or income averaging, work experience should be entered continuously for the number of years worked. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Clarification on instructions given in "implied status letters" -- REP-2021-0134
threads.question:
Hello,
I am writing to seek clarification on the instructions given to applicants who are applying for work or study permits in Canada. I have attached the letter for your reference. It refers to R186(u) IRPR, which at the time of this writing this email, provides:
186 A foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit
(u) until a decision is made on an application made by them under subsection 201(1), if they have remained in Canada after the expiry of their work permit and they have continued to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, other than the expiry date;
But two statements in the letter contradict R186(u):
1) “..you are authorized to continue working with the same conditions until June 01, 2021 or until a decision is made on your application, whichever is first."
2) “this extended period of work is authorized as per subsection 186(u) of the IRPR."
R186(u) does not specify a validity date for implied status. I would argue that no such legislative provision exists to restrict the period of implied status (until June 1 or any other date). Likewise, an extension should not be applicable for the same reason.
I would very much appreciate your clarification on the above, if my understanding of the existing legislation is incorrect.
Thank you for your attention.
threads.answer:
Hello,
QuESTioN: R186(u) does not specify a validity date for implied status. I would argue that no such legislative provision exists to restrict the period of implied status (until June 1 or any other date). Likewise, an extension should not be applicable for the same reason.
I would very much appreciate your clarification on the above, if my understanding of the existing legislation is incorrect.
RESPoNSE: Please note that the 'interim proof of authority to work' letter is only provided to applicants who are renewing
work permits. There is no similar letter for applicants applying to renew their study permit.
The status in not implied’ but maintained if the work permit renewal application is submitted prior to the expiry of their existing work permit. Yes, you are correct in that the Regulations state that the period of authorized stay is extended until a decision is made and that a person who is applying to renew their work permit will have authority to work under R186(u) until a decision is made as long as they continue under existing work permit conditions or unless they leave Canada.
The letter is provided to applicants as proof that they have continued authority to work and the date is added to give employers and other stakeholders a more concrete period of time of authorized work. IRCC has found in the past that employers and stakeholders are reluctant to accept an unknown period such as until a decision is made'. Should the application not be processed within the date on the letter clients may contact IRCC to request continued proof if needed. In addition, there is no requirement that the applicant must present this letter to anyone it is only provided as a service to the client.
The letter has a 120 day validity that corresponds with IRCC Service Standard for in-Canada applications. Historically, IRCC meets our service standard more than 90% of the time. During the initial COVID-19 pandemic period the processing tine has gone beyond our service standard. However, IRCC has reduced our current processing time back to the service standard.
The letter also indicates that : This extended period of work is authorized as per subsection 186(u) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. This statement would provide the evidence that they can continue working until a decision is made.
For clarity: the applicant may continue working until a decision is made if they meet all the requirements of R1 86(u) regardless of the date in the letter. The letter is simply a document to provide surety to employers and other stakeholders that the applicant may continue working.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Electronic Signatures & Remote Commissioning-Presentation to LSO on March 8, 2021 -- REP-2021-0010
threads.question:
Dear ImmRep:
What is IRCC's policy on electronic signatures and remote commissioning?
Will IRCC accept a digital signature or a copied and pasted signature on forms such as the Use of Representative or Family Information form? Many applicants don't have access to a printer during COVID, also the IRCC tech team has tweeted that the electronic signature at the end of an application is sufficient (contrary to the information in the instruction guide)
IRCC's newest form the IMMo006 Application for Authorization to Travel to Canada explicitly requires a digital signature.
Will IRCC accept documents that have been remotely commissioned, such as the Stat Dec of CL Union? This is in line with most provincial legislation that is now authorizing lawyers to remotely commission documents.
I am speaking at the Law Society of Ontario on this topic on March 8, 2021 and would appreciate an answer if possible in
advance of my presentation.
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your enquiry. As is outlined on our website, a physical or scanned signature is not required for online application forms.
Clients can simply upload the required documents to their account. After they have uploaded all the necessary forms, a “next” button will appear at the bottom of the page. Once clicked, clients will be prompted to enter their name as it appears on their application form, and answer a security question which, together, will be understood as their electronic signature for the entirety of their application.

Applicants who apply for a work permit while holding implied status, meaning they submitted an application to extend or change their status to visitor or student before the expiry date of their study permít and no decision had been made at the time of the submission of their PGWP application, are not considered to have applied for a work permit before the expiry of their study permit according to paragraph R186(w)(ii). threads.answer:

You can work full-time until we make a decision on your work permit application if you
- had a valid study permit when you submitted your application
- completed your study program

threads.subject: EXPRESS ENTRY: CRS points for arranged employment - "currently working in Canada" question -- REP- 2020-2412
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: We would like to seek clarification on how CEC candidates should go about indicating their offer of employment in the IRCC portal when they submit their Express Entry profile in situations where they normally work in Canada, they are temporarily overseas but not comfortable travelling back to Canada immediately due to COVID. They continue to work remotely for a Canadian employer for whom they have worked for over a year in Canada and will return to as soon as travel is more practicable. In reviewing the Ministerial Instructions with respect to the Express Entry System and the corresponding Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), we noticed that such a scenario does not fall outside of the “arranged employment” definition but there is a gap in the EE portal because this situation of a foreign national who has a valid job offer while being temporarily overseas does not seem to be contemplated. A foreign national does not appear to be required to be physically in Canada at the time of claiming the “arranged employment" points as long as they meet all other requirements (they worked in Canada for a year already, have a valid employer-specific work permit, currently working for that employer (there is a mention that they must be working for that same employer but there is no specific exclusion of remote work nor is there a qualifier such as "in Canada"), and they have an offer for at least one continuous year after it is expected their PR visa is issued. As such, our interpretation is that a candidate who has a valid LMlA-exempt work permit, has worked in Canada for at least one year in the last 10 years and has an ongoing job offer for continuous work in Canada once they arrive back in Canada, would have to answer “yes" to the question about current work in Canada in order to get prompted to answer the questions that are relevant to the 29(2)(a) definition of arranged employment. Although this does not factually represent the current situation of a work permit holder working outside of Canada due to COVID, we submit that this should be an appropriate temporary measure, provided that the candidate has proof of their previous one year of work experience in Canada based on that work permit, the work permit is still valid and the employer continues to offer them employment in Canada. Please let us know whether IRCC would consider revising the EE application portal to better reflect the fact that the temporary remote work outside of Canada does not preclude a candidate from claiming arranged employment points if all other criteria under section 29(2) of the Mls are met. Otherwise, we will proceed to answer the question “incorrectly” in the portal and properly explain the unique situation in detail in the representative's cover letter.
Answer: Express Entry's arranged employment points are modelled on the arranged employment provisions in section 82(1) and section 82(2)(a) of the regulations for Federal Skilled Workers in IRPA, which references both employment in Canada, and the applicant being physically in Canada to receive CRS points for arranged employment. IRCC's treatment of arranged employment must be consistent across the regulations and the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions. If the applicant's job offer is recognized for a worker currently established outside Canada, the Immigration Officer must be satisfied that the applicant intends to become a permanent resident (establishing in Canada and meeting the residency obligations). The intent of this type of job offer is to make permanent residence more accessible to skilled workers who have demonstrated the ability to integrate into the Canadian labour market. The purpose of the Canadian work experience requirement is to select workers who can economically integrate in Canada, which is demonstrated in part by the accumulation of 1,560 hours of continuous, skilled Canadian work experience on their employer-specific work permit. Remote work does not constitute Canadian work experience and would therefore not count for the job offer.
We would recommend that the applicant request a Permanent Residence LMIA from ESDC to support the job offer, which is free of charge. If the applicant chooses to proceed with the course of action outlined in your email (“to answer the question “incorrectly" in the portal and properly explain the unique situation in detail in the representative's cover letter”), the onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer.

If an Express Entry candidate is issued an ITA under CEC before they actually have the 1-year of valid Canadian work experience, can they still submit an application for permanent residence as long as the application is submitted after having completed their 1-year of valid Canadian work experience?

threads.subject: Examination of Residency Obligation-- REP-2020-0373
threads.question:
Greetings,
Amid the introduction of the Exit/Entry Program in cooperation with the CBSA, we have the following questions regarding residency obligation that need your kind clarification.
A28(2)(b) prescribes the level of sufficiency required of a PR when demonstrating compliance with his/her residency obligation during an examination. In our observation, there are no provisions specifying the level of sufficiency required of a PR when demonstrating compliance outside of an examination. Therefore, we are wondering if there are any circumstances where PRs can be required to demonstrate compliance with his/her residency obligation, when not being subject to an examination that 's described under A15(1)? If such circumstances exist, what is the level of sufficiency required in those cases?
Also in our observation, officers have the authority to prepare an inadmissibility report under A44(1) against a PR for non- compliance with the residency obligation, but the preparation of such a report does not necessarily need to result from a prior examination. Therefore, can an officer lawfully prepare an inadmissibility report under A44(1) against a PR in Canada who is not
subject to an examination, for non-compliance with residency obligation, based on the information obtained from CBSA under the Exit/Entry Program?
Your clarification is greatly appreciated.
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your patience with our responses to this inquiry.
As IRPA 18(3) explains, "Even though a person seeking to enter Canada is not, in accordance with regulations made under subsection 26(2), required to appear for an examination, an officer may require the person to do so." There may be occurrences when an officer may require a person to demonstrate compliance with his/her residency obligation and the provisions would remain the same as when the person is subject to an examination.
IRPA A44(1) allows an officer to prepare an inadmissibility report in relation to a permanent resident or a foreign national "who is in Canada". The procedural requirements and legal obligations related to gathering information from the person for the purpose of writing an A44(1) report will depend on whether the person is still subject to examination Pursuant to A15(1), individuals who make applications under the IRPA are subject to an examination for various reasons, including to determine whether that person has a right to enter Canada or may become authorized to enter or remain in Canada pursuant to A18(1).

threads.subject: H&C application for PRRA applicants from ADR or TSR countries -- REP-2021-0027
threads.question:
From Dear Madam, Sir,
I have a question about eligibility to submit an H&C application under sec. 25 IRPA I am hoping you can assist me with.
In cases where individuals from countries that fall under an ADR (administrative deferral of removal) or TSR (temporary suspension of removal) enter Canada and are referred for a PRRA because they are not eligible to claim refugee protection (for any number of reasons), the CBSA will not contact them to start their PRRA process as they are not considered "removal ready" (since they cannot be returned to their country of origin). As such, these individuals can remain for a number of years in limbo, as most ofthe countries on these 2 lists have not been removed or changed in many years.
Art. 25(1.01) and (1.2) IRPA indicates that a person that made a claim for refugee protection or an application for protection is restricted from submitted an H&C application. Does this article also apply to potential PRRA applicants who fall under this category of individuals from countries on either the ADR or TSR lists that might never get called in to start their PRRA applications as they cannot be considered "removal ready"? What other process or application would they qualify for in order to obtain permanent status based on their ongoing establishment in
Canada while waiting for the opportunity to explain their fear of return?
I thank you in advance for your attention to my enquiry and look forward to your response.
Sincerely,
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Dear
Q. In your request you ask whether the restrictions from submitting an H&C application under 25(1.01) and (1.2) apply to potential PRRA applicants from countries on either the ADR (administrative deferral of removal) or TSR (temporary suspension of removal) list.
Response
Subsection 25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) allows for an individual to make an application for permanent residence based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations (H&C application) to the Minister. Nevertheless, as you noted in your enquiry, there are restrictions and exceptions to this.
These restrictions and exceptions are not affected by whether an individual comes from a country under an ADR or a TSR. Instead, these restrictions and exceptions apply only to individuals who fit the conditions described by the clauses in the legislation, regardless of whether they come from a country under an ADR/TSR or not. To determine whether these restrictions and exceptions apply in the case you have brought forth, one must review the relevant sections ofIRPA and see whether they apply.
In reviewing your enquiry, it appears that the most relevant section ofIRPA to consider is 25(1.2)(b.1) which notes:
The minister may not examine the request if (b.1) the foreign national made a claim for refugee protection that was determined to be ineligible to be referred to the Refugee Protection Division and they made an application for protection to the Minister that is pending;
To fit under the exception described in 25(1.2)(b.1) ofIRPA, the individuals would need to have been found ineligible to have their claim referred to the Refugee Protection Division and, they would need to have filed a PRRA application that is still before the Minister. However, if the CBSA has not contacted the individuals to notify them of their opportunity to submit a PRRA application and, more specifically, if the individuals have not yet submitted their PRRA application, they would not fall under the exception described in 25(1.2)(b.1) and would still be able to make a request for H&C consideration under 25(1).
From the description provided in your enquiry, it would appear that the individuals were found ineligible to have their claims referred to the Refugee Protection Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board. However, as you state that CBSA has not contacted the individuals yet to start their PRRA process, it would appear that they have not yet filed a PRRA application. If this is the case, then, based on this limited information, these individuals would still be eligible to file an H&C application.
Q. You also ask what other processes they would qualify for in order to obtain permanent status based on their ongoing
mmigration, Refugees nmigration, Réfugiés establishment in Canada while waiting for the opportunity to explain their fear of return.
Various different pathways towards permanent residence exist, each with their own requirements. Which pathway is the best fit depends on a person’s individual circumstances.
While IRCC cannot advise on individual cases, ongoing establishment in Canada is one of various factors taken into consideration when assessing an application for permanent residence based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
However, if the individuals have temporary resident status in Canada and meet the other minimum requirements (including employment, language, or educational requirements), the individuals may be eligible to apply under various economic classes such as the Provincial Nominee class or the Canadian Experience Class.
Background
A more full review of the most relevant restrictions and exceptions to section 25(1) ofIRPA follows.
According to subsection 25(1.01) ofIRPA, a designated foreign national may not make a request under subsection 25(1) until five years after the day:
- a final determination is made on their claim in the case of someone who filed a refugee claim but has not filed an application for protection (PRRA application);
- a final determination is made on their application for protection in the case of someone who has made an application for protection (PRRA application); or
- on which they become a designated foreign national in any other case.
It is important to emphasize that the restrictions set out in subsection 25(1.01) above do not apply to all foreign nationals. They only apply to persons who fit the definition of a designated foreign national as set out in subsection 20.1(2) ofIRPA. Thus, for persons found to be a designated foreign national, there is a five year restriction from applying for H&C consideration. However, if the individual does not fit the definition of a designated foreign national as set out in 20.1(2) of IRPA, then the restrictions in subsection 25(1.01) do not apply to them.
In looking at the specifics of the case you have put forth, there is insufficient information to determine whether the foreign nationals in question are designated foreign nationals as defined under subsection 20.1(2) of IRPA and whether the restriction under 25(1.01) applies in this case. However, as Section 20.1 is not often invoked, it is not likely that this restriction applies in this case.
Similarly, subsection 25(1.2) sets out the exceptions to subsection 25(1). These are cases where the Minister may not examine an H&C application made under 25(1). Most relevant to this enquiry appear to be paragraphs 25(1.2)(b) through (c). Paragraphs 25(1.2)(b) and (b.1) note that the Minister may not examine a request for H&C consideration made under subsection 25(1) if
the person is a foreign national who still has a claim for refugee protection before either the Refugee Protection Division or the Refugee Appeal Division; the person is a foreign national who made a refugee claim that was determined to be ineligible to be referred to the Refugee Protection Division and then that same person made a PRRA application that is still before the Minister.
Paragraph 25(1.2)(c) refers to a 12 month bar on applications for H&C consideration; however, this bar only applies to foreign
nmigration, Réfugiés
nationals who's refugee claim was rejected or determined withdrawn after substantive evidence was heard.
Again, in looking at the specifics of your case, you refer to, “individuals... [who] enter Canada and are referred for a PRRA because they are not eligible to claim refugee protection... [but] the CBSA will not contact them to start their PRRA process as they are not considered "removal ready"...". As these individual were deemed ineligible to have their claims referred to the Immigration and Refugee Board, it cannot be said that they still have a claim pending before either the Refugee Protection Division or the Refugee Appeal Division. Similarly, it cannot be said that substantive evidence on their claim was heard. Thus, the exceptions under 25(1.2)(b) and (c) do not apply.
To fit under the exception described in 25(1.2)(b.1) ofIRPA, the individuals would need to have been found ineligible to have their claim referred to the Refugee Protection Division and, they would need to have filed a PRRA application that is still before the Minister. However, if the CBSA has not contacted the individuals to notify them of their opportunity to submit a PRRA application or if the individuals have not yet submitted their PRRA application, they would not fall under the exception described in 25(1.2)(b.1) and would still be able to make a request for H&C consideration under 25(1).
Again, as you note that the CBSA has not contacted these individuals to start their PRRA process, then it would appear that these individuals do not fall under the exception described in 25(1.2)(b.1). Instead, the individuals would still be able to make a request for H&C consideration under 25(1).
Hoping the above information addresses your concerns.
Sincerely,

threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: There are certain trades such as Electricians, Automotive service technicians that require mandatory licensing before working in that field with those designations. However, in order to be eligible for the licensing one needs to first complete an apprenticeship and then after completing apprenticeship hours become eligible to write the licensing exam. Under Canadian Experience Class, we understand that the employment requirements are not necessarily are required to be met. Can an applicant applying under CEC, claim points for a trade NOC such as an automotive service technician Apprentice or Electrician apprentice without being registered with the trade school? Some trade school and some trades require few hours of training as well before being able to register for the apprenticeship program as well. Kindly advise, if a CEC candidate is able to claim experience successfully under a trade NOC as an apprentice without the necessary licensing or registering with the trade school as an apprentice.
Answer: Yes, an Express Entry candidate would be able to claim apprenticeship work experience under the Canadian Experience Class, as long the work experience also meets all other criteria of the program. This includes having at least 12 months of full time (or the equivalent of part-time) Canadian skilled work experience in one of more NOC O, A, or B occupations within the 36 months before the date of application receipt, as per 87.1(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. The work experience must have been gained by working in Canada under temporary resident status with authorization to work and be remunerated by the payment of wages or a commission. Any period of employment gained when the applicant was in full-time studies does not count towards work experience for this program. Additionally, during that period of employment, the applicant must have:
- performed the actions described in the lead statement for the occupation(s) as set out in the occupational description of the NOC [R87.1(2)(b)]; and
- performed a substantial number of the main duties, including all the essential duties, of the occupation(s) as set out in the occupational description of the NOC [R87.1(2)(c)].

# Hello,
Foreign nationals may study in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study as long as it is 6 months or less in duration. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (i.e., up to 6 months).
A professional training program is a type of additional education or training usually offered to professionals already in the field. Professional development is generally “accredited"; that is, it is recognized by an industry, association, or profession. Professional training is offered through community colleges, universities, CEGEPs, career colleges, professional associations, or unions.
In general, professional training programs require participants to complete both a study and work component in order to successfully complete the program, and obtain the given credential. However, unlike co-op/internship programs in post- secondary institutions (e.g., universities, community colleges) such programs often consist of a full-time work component and a part-time study component. The work component often comprises more than 50% of the study component.
Applicants wishing to participate in professional training programs must apply for a study permit to cover the study portion, if the study component is more than six months at a designated learning institution; and apply for the appropriate work permit if there is a work portion. More information can be found here: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/other-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/other-) considerations.html

threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
An applicant completes a three-year college program in Canada. Subsequently, they complete a bachelor’s degree outside of Canada. They receive an educational credential assessment for that degree which states it is from a recognized institution and is equivalent to a Canadian degree. Credits from the college degree are applied towards the bachelor's degree, allowing the applicant to complete the degree in less than the standard amount of time (say two years instead of three).
How many points would be awarded for education? Would it be based on a bachelor's degree, (120 points if single) or on ‘Two or more certificates, diplomas, or degrees. One must be for a program of three or more years' (128 points if single).
Answer:
A candidate will only be awarded education points under the Comprehensive Ranking System and the Federal Skilled Worker selection grid for having 'two or more post-secondary program credentials' if the educational credentials represent separate certificates, diplomas or degrees. To get points for having two or more post-secondary credentials, at least one of the credentials must be for three or more years of study.
Based on the information provided, the applicant should declare only a single post-secondary program credential of three years or more. This is because they did not complete a three year program then another program. The first program became the Bachelor's. Therefore, the applicant should input only their Bachelor's Degree and the appropriate points will be awarded.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Ma question concerne le programme cité en objet. Je comprends que la demande doit être envoyée par la poste. La liste de contrôle des documents ne semble laisser qu’une seule option concernant les formulaires : les originaux sont exigés. Ma question : Est-ce qu’une demande sera jugée incomplète et retournée au demandeur si des copies des formulaires sont envoyées? Je pense notamment aux membres de la famille ou personnes à charge d’un demandeur qui se trouvent hors du Canada. Il est possible que ces personnes se trouvent dans des pays où les conditions sont extrêmement difficiles et qu’il soit périlleux, voire impossible, d’effectuer l’envoi vers le Canada des formulaires originaux. La même question s’applique aux photos format passeport de ces personnes hors du Canada.
Tel que vous le mentionnez, la Liste de contrôle des documents (IMM 1015) indique que les formulaires originaux doivent être fournis.
Toutefois, notez que des instructions ont été publiées pour la période de pandémie de COVID-19. Ainsi, si une nouvelle demande ne contient pas tous les documents à l’appui (les frais connexes sont exigés), le demandeur doit joindre à sa demande une explication démontrant qu'il est touché par l’interruption des services découlant du nouveau coronavirus.
À noter que les demandes jugées incomplètes qui ne sont pas accompagnées d’une explication, ou pour des raisons sans lien avecl’interruption des services découlant des incidences du nouveau coronavirus, peuvent être rejetées aux termes de l’article R10, et les frais associés à la demande seront remboursés au demandeur. Le motif du rejet ne doit pas être lié à l’interruption des services.
Ainsi, pendant cette période, si une demande est soumise avec des photocopies des formulaires signés ou sans les photos format passeport requises, les demandes ne seront pas retournées. Les orignaux de même que les photos doivent être soumis à une date ultérieure, lorsque cela est raisonnablement possible.
Si les documents sont manquants pour des raisons exceptionnelles et non liées aux incidences du coronavirus, veuillez également fournir des explications et, si possible, des preuves à l’appui. L'évaluation se fera au cas par cas.
Pour plus de détails, consultez les pages suivantes : Résidence permanente : Exécution des programmes sur la COVID-19; Comment présenter une demande?; Guide 1016-Guide de demande pour la voie d’accès à la résidence permanente des travailleurs de la santé (pandémie de COVID-19).

For IRCC purposes, police certificates have no expiry dates. Applicants are requested to submit a police certificate for countries they have resided for more than 6 months since the age of 18 along with their application for permanent residence. As with any case, the officer reviewing the file may require a new police certificate in order to be satisfied that the applicant is not criminally inadmissible.

Should your client experience such challenge, please provide a written justification outlining these circumstances and also include documentary evidence supporting this claim. threads.subject: Implied status as a worker while waiting for specific work permit as a home child care provider--REP-2020- 1822
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
I would like to request for some insights on a situation where a person is on PGWP. As per regulation a foreign national can be on implied status as a temporary resident if an application is completed/submitted before the expiry of his/her current status.
In the case of a PGWP holder who found a job offer under the home child care provider pilot and completed/submitted a PR application and at the same time specific work permit as a home child care provider before his pgwp expires, will he also merit the implied status as a worker and can continue working while waiting for the said work permit ?
Pls. clarify with regulations.
Thank you.
Best regards,
threads.answer:
Dear
Our sincere apologies for the delay in our response.
Question: In the case of a PGwP holder who found a job offer under the home child care provider pilot and completed/submitted a PR application and at the same time specific work permit as a home child care provider before his pgwp expires, will he also merit the implied status as a worker and can continue working while waiting for the said work permit ?
Response: Please note that the Immigration Representatives Mailbox will only reply to general immigration program or policy related enquiries and cannot comment on specific cases. We are replying based on the general scenario that you have described.
A temporary resident must apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, their period of authorized stay as a temporary resident is extended by law until a decision is made [R183(5)]. Such a person is considered to have maintained their status (sometimes referred to as implied status) as a temporary resident during that period. If a temporary resident applies for renewal of their work or study permit and their permit expires before a decision is made, paragraph 186(u) and section 189 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) (the right to continue working or studying under the same conditions pending a determination of their application for renewal) apply only as long as the person remains in Canada.
Therefore, a caregiver would have maintained status as long as the HCCP/HSW permanent residence application (including an HCCP/HSW occupation-restricted open work permit application) is submitted before the expiry of the current work permit.
However, individuals who are on temporary status in Canada may consider submitting a separate work permit application or an extension of their existing work permit under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) or the International Mobility Program (IMP), even if they have already applied under the HCCP/HSW pilots. Permanent residence (PR) applications take longer to process and the COVID-19 pandemic has caused more delays. This affects when IRCC can issue the work permit related to the PR application. Even though they will have maintained status, it may be harder to get some government services or benefits. Also, if their PR application is refused, rejected for being incomplete, or returned for being over that year's cap, we'll return the related work permit application as well. If this happens: they'll lose their maintained status if they are not eligible to restore their status, they'd have to leave Canada

threads.subject: Applying for Permanent Residence outside Canada-Relocating to Canada on WP prior to decision on PR --
threads.question:
REP-2021-0050
Hello,
Question:
1. A foreign national created their profile in the Express Entry pool as a Federal Skilled Worker, received their Invitation to Apply and submitted an Application for Permanent Residency while residing outside of Canada. As this foreign national is also in receipt of a positive LMiA and pre-approved Work Permit, can s/he enter Canada and await the processing of their PR application while on lawful status as a worker in Canada?
2. If yes to the above, who would need to be notified of this change? And via webform?
Response:
Under the current rules governing travel restrictions, foreign nationals who hold a valid work permit or were issued a port of entry decision letter on their work permit application may be eligible to enter Canada. Officers will assess the work permit application against the job offer –the job offer must be valid and a position exists. If a job offer is provided in order for the foreign national to travel to Canada, i.e., to overcome travel restrictions, and the officer determines/finds that there is no actual job waiting, the work permit application may be refused.
Before boarding travellers, airlines must be satisfied that a foreign national is exempt from the travel prohibition. An approved PR must present a valid COPR dated pre-March 18, along with other relevant travel documentation. They can't board by virtue of having a COPR issued after March 18th, but if they have a work permit and can enter, then they stay in Canada and wait for their PR to be processed.
A PR applicant who received an ITA for PR through Express Entry and has a port of entry letter on their work permit application and a permanent job offer with an LMIA can enter Canada as a TR (not as a PR). The foreign national must meet the travel exemptions related to foreign workers in the OiC and have a genuine job offer.
If the foreign national managed to enter into Canada by virtue of their work permit, they should notify IRCC of their new address via the IRCC Webform.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:

Question: What is the proper procedure to follow when an individual has received an ITA under Express Entry and they cannot produce their non-accompanying dependents for a medical examination because they do not have custody of the minor child and the child's other parent is not co-operating? there are humanitarian and compassionate reasons why the non-accompanying dependent could not be examined. The
applicant would need to make the case for an A25 H&C exemption and the officer will determine if the case is sufficient to warrant an exemption from the requirement that the dependent be examined. Would that applicant be meeting the MEC under R87.1(1) if s/he intends to live elsewhere in Canada but still remotely working for a Quebec-based company? For example: planning to live and settle in Toronto, ON, but still working remotely for a Quebec-based company?
Answer: Applicants can use work experience gained in Quebec to apply for Express Entry (all programs) however, officers must be satisfied that the applicant does not intend to reside in Quebec. The onus remains on the applicant to satisfy the officer per subsection 16(1) of the Act, that they truthfully intend to reside outside Quebec. Given the applicant is working remotely for a Quebec company, the officer must also be satisfied that the applicant is capable of doing the job without having to reside in Quebec.
An officer may exercise their discretion and request further documentation such as, but not limited to, lease/rental/purchase agreements, letters of support, etc., in order to satisfy them of the applicant's intent to reside outside of Quebec. We suggest you provide any supporting documentation along with the application. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:

Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: My question relates to arranged employment as awarded under the CRS points grid. I have read the Ministerial Instructions but they don't cover this specific scenario: An applicant receives arranged employment points for having a LMiA (and had a LMIA-based work permit at the time of application). The applicant applies for and receives a bridging open work permit while their PR application continues to process. The applicant then changes jobs using their BOWP.
Is the applicant required to obtain a new LMIA and LMIA-based work permit from the new employer to maintain their arranged employment points? (The Ministerial Instructions address the scenario of losing employment but not changing employment).
Answer: As long as the applicant had arranged employment at the time of the Invitation to Apply (ITA) and at the submission of their electronic application for permanent residence (e-APR), the applicant will not lose their CRS points for arranged employment, as defined under section 29 of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system. Express Entry candidates are responsible for ensuring that the information in their profile is up-to-date at all times, so any changes in circumstance (including a new job) should be communicated via their profile. Please note that a change in employers may have an impact if the applicant is applying under the Federal Skilled Worker program (FSW). More information about arranged employment and FSW can be found on our website.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox
