threads.subject: Clarification on Sponsor and Co-signer eligibility -- REP-2021-0167
threads.question:
To whom it may concern,
With respect to parents and grandparents sponsorship I understand that the co-signer should only be the spouse or the common law partner of the sponsor.
In the case of a separated spouse with no legal separation papers or document nor divorce, and is still married. They declared that they are separated for three consecutive years due to relationship breakdown. However, the co-signer is willing to sign the
sponsorship undertaking considering that they have two children together with the sponsor.
The question is can they proceed with the application to sponsor the parents ? the sponsor was fortunate to get into the draw, though she did it herself without having a counsel. Can you please enlighten this situation. Your advice is greatly appreciated. Thank you very much.
Respectfully,
and Cizenship Canadaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Even if the sponsor is separated from their spouse (regardless of legal papers or the duration of the separation), unless they are divorced, they are still considered spouses of one another and therefore, a separated spouse can co-sign the sponsorship application.
It should be noted that a co-signer is equally responsible as the sponsor to provide basic requirements: food, clothing, shelter, fuel, utilities, household supplies, personal requirements and other goods and services, including dental care, eye care and other health needs not provided by public health care to the sponsored person. In addition, the co-signer is bound by the undertaking, and remains responsible for their relative(s) for the duration specified for the applicable family class category, which is 20 years for the parents and grandparents program.
We hope you find this information useful.
Thank you,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox (IRCC)

Because the parents and grandparents program opened later than usual for 2020, sponsors were invited to apply early in 2021. Because of this, (IRCC) assess sponsors on their income for tax years 2020, 2019 and 2018.
Since many sponsors may have been affected financially by the COVID-19 pandemic, the income requirement for the 2020 tax year has been reduced to the minimum necessary income, instead of the minimum necessary income plus 30%. - regular Employment Insurance benefits (rather than just special Employment Insurance benefits)

- other temporary COVID-19 related benefits o as long as they're not part of provincial social assistance programs
Note: This does not affect the income requirements for the 2019 and 2018 tax years.

threads.subject: [URGENT] Worker/ student -> out of status -> restore to visitor? -- REP-2020-2199
threads.question:
Hello,
Initial Question (REP-2020-2497): IRCC authorizes out-of-status students to apply for a post-graduation work permit by including restoration fees with their PGWP application.
Would IRCC similarly authorize an out-of-status student to apply for an LMIA-exempt open work permit (specifically under LMIA exemption codes C-42 or C-41) by including a restoration to student fee receipt with their application? If not, what would be the correct procedure?
Response: Study permit holders who do not apply for a PGWP before their study permit expires would be in Canada without a valid status. Their temporary resident status would need to be restored as a student before they can be issued a PGWP. In this situation, the procedure is to submit an application to restore status as a student and apply for a PGWP simultaneously and submit their proof of completion of studies and transcripts instead of their old letter of acceptance (please note that a new letter of acceptance is not required). Note that they must pay the fees for a new study permit and a work permit, which will include restoration fee ($200), study permit fee ($150), work permit fee ($155) and open work permit holder fee ($100).
As the applications are submitted simultaneously, they are processed together at the processing center. As such, a decision on the Post-Graduation Work permit will be rendered likely on the same day as the study permit, unless additional documents are required.
Please note that an applicant may only restore to an authorization that they held immediately prior to the restoration application, as per section 182 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. In the case of an out-of-status student, the applicant may only restore their authorization to study and not to work. As well as the study permit fee, the applicant must also submit the standard application package for a study permit (Please see Guide 5552 - Applying to Change Conditions or Extend Your Stay in Canada-Student).
The applicant may also choose to submit an application for a work permit under a different category instead of applying for a PGWP (e.g. one under LMIA exemption code C41 or C42) at the same time if they qualify for another type of work permit. If an officer determines that the applicant is eligible for restoration as a student, only then will they assess the work permit application.
For more information, please see: Restoration of temporary resident status
Follow-up Question (REP-2020-2592): There is conflicting information available regarding whether a foreign national who held status as a worker/student when he/she fell out of status eligible to restore their status to visitor?
If so, are two forms required? i.e. in the worker scenario, both application form for restoration as worker (IMM5710) and visitor (IMM5708) are required to be submitted via portal and the fees paid twice?
In the past, CPC-E has approved applications corresponding to the above-mentioned scenarios with only the submission of
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
the application for restoration as a visitor (IMM5708). However, the current restoration guidelines, modified on April 8, 2020, state that "a foreign national can only apply to restore their status and authorization to one they held immediately prior to the need to apply for restoration."
Please confirm if these guidelines now preclude restoring to a lower status and if not, how many forms are required to be submitted.

The program delivery instructions regarding restoration (linked above)
specify the following:
It is important to note that an applicant can only restore to an authorization that they held immediately prior to the restoration application. As an example, a student who lost their status cannot apply to restore status with authorization as a worker.
A restoration application is submitted with the purpose of restoring the applicant's status as a temporary resident; as per the above, they are limited to seek their authorization (i.e. as a worker or student) to what they previously held. An out-of-status worker or student may apply to restore their status as a visitor without submitting an application (and the associated fees) for a work or study permit. However, restoring their status as a visitor may limit them to later apply for a work or study permit from inside Canada.

threads.answer:

Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Due to the impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic on our operations, we have experienced delays in providing a response.
As you have mentioned, IRCC deems the Somali passport unreliable and not valid for travel to Canada. An alternative solution would be for the family member to obtain a valid travel document. A sponsor and their family member(s) must meet all of the applicable requirements as set out in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and it's applicable Regulations (IRPR). This includes meeting the requirement stipulated in section 50(1) of the IRPR. Foreign nationals who do not meet the requirements of the IRPA or the IRPR may make a written request for consideration under subsection A25(1) for humanitarian and compassionate considerations. The foreign national would need to provide a written request along with their family class application in order to be considered under these grounds. Requests for humanitarian and compassionate considerations are assessed on a case- by-case basis. This means that the deciding officer will assess the request and all the relevant information in order to determine whether a special grant of an exemption from a requirement of the IRPA or IRPR is warranted. Question Retail butchers are one of the eligible occupations under the Agri-Food Pilot Project. Do retail butchers working for supermarket meat/butcher departments qualify? My concern is whether a supermarket/employer is considered to be operating under NAICS 3116, one of the eligible industries under the Pilot. NAICS 3116 is comprised of "establishments primarily engaged in manufacturing meat products". The typical supermarket meat department is engaged in processing of meat products, including receiving animal carcasses and butchering the carcasses into consumer-friendly cuts. However, typical supermarkets also sell produce and other non-meat food products.
[https://www23.statcan.gc.ca/imdb/p3VD.pl?](https://www23.statcan.gc.ca/imdb/p3VD.pl?) Function=getVD&TVD= &CVD= &CPV=3116&CST=01012012&CLV=3&MLV=5
Answer
Applicants applying to the Agri-Food Pilot (AFP) program will need to demonstrate that they meet the minimum work experience requirement in one or more eligible combinations of the National Occupational Classification (NOC) and North American Industry Classification System (NAICS). Activities under eligible industry NAICS 3116 (Meat product manufacturing) lists the eligible occupation NOC 6331 (Butchers, meat cutter, and fishmongers in retail and wholesale). That said, grocery stores and supermarkets fall under NAICS 4451 which is not eligible under the AFP program.
Please note that the officer would need to be satisfied that the applicant has performed the main job duties, including all of the essential duties listed under the NOC 6331 and that the employer's principal business activity is consistent with NAICS 3116.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Please see our response to your question.
Question: If an applicant obtains a LMIA exempt work permit restricted to a city (e.g. Montreal) but want to move to another city that is not in the same administrative region (e.g.), what would be the best way forward? Would they require a new work permit?
The employer operates an office in the city mentioned on the work permit and the employee will be working remotely for the employer within the same provide.
Please confirm how to proceed in situations like this as we believe this is something that we might see more and more.
Answer: There are two sets of conditions to consider in employment location – those imposed on the employee under section 185 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) and those imposed on the employer under 209.3 of the IRPR. If the location is imposed on the work permit, the foreign worker must change their conditions to move locations.
For foreign workers working remotely on a temporary basis due to the Covid situation, it is recommended that employers submit a voluntary disclosure to notify IRCC of the changes.
For scenarios where an employer wishes to make teleworking permanent and valid post-Covid, we recommend that the employer submit a new offer of employment and have the worker submit an application to change conditions as a worker.
We would also recommend that employers include teleworking arrangement information in any new offer of employment. The employer is also required to maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at the time of inspection.
If the employer believes that they are not meeting conditions, they can use the voluntary disclosure process.
We hope this information is of assistance.

Question: My concern relates to the co-founders for the SUV applicants. Will the co-founders' PR applications continue to be processed if the other founder proceeds with an Express Entry application?
Answer: If the applicant obtains permanent residence through Express Entry, their SUV application will be withdrawn. If the applicant was deemed an “essential" person under the SUV application, the remaining SUV candidates would be refused for not meeting the requirements to be a member of the start-up business class. Alternatively, the other applications may be returned if processing has not yet commenced.
However, if the applicant was not deemed an “essential” person under the SUV application, their shares of the company would then be re-classified under “other shareholders” and the remaining applicants and the designated entity would need to jointly hold more than 50% of the total voting rights to remain eligible in the program. The remaining applicants may need to provide a new Commitment Certificate and Letter of Support, and additional documentation noting the changes in ownership and shareholders.
The assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements. Please inform us of any changes or decisions made using the IRCC Webform as new documents may be required.
We trust that this information will assist you.

Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives
Question: I have a client who has been recently been approved Dual Intent LMIA (supports Work Permit and Permanent Residence) from ESDC for the position of Retail Manager, a skill level B position, corresponding to NOC 0621. The client has a valid Express Entry profile with a CRS score of 425. I have the following questions. Is it mandatory for the TFW to come on a work permit to Canada to claim 50 points towards a valid job offer? Can TFW claim 50 points on his Express Entry profile for a
Answer: No, it is not mandatory for the applicant to be on a work permit to claim arranged employment points. The applicant would only be granted 50 CRS points for arranged employment if he meets one of the requirements under 29(2) of the Ministerial Instructions for Express Entry. However, as per 29(3), if the foreign national is unable to perform the duties of the employment or is unlikely to perform them, then the applicant would no longer be entitled to these 50 CRS points. The officer assessing the application must be satisfied that the applicant will be coming to Canada to perform the job stated in their application. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
Question: The client applies for a work permit based on a positive dual intent LMIA but if the work permit is refused by the visa office abroad, can the TFW still claim 50 points towards a valid job offer for the positive dual intent LMIA?
Answer: Yes, the applicant can still claim 50 CRS points for arranged employment as long as they continue to meet 29(2) of the Ministerial Instructions for Express Entry. However, if the offer is revoked or ceases to be a qualifying offer of arranged employment, the applicant is no longer entitled to the 50 CRS points and will be adjusted accordingly.

threads.question:
1*1and Cizenship Canada
Dear Imm Reps,
If a foreign national holds an LMIA exempt work permit for a one-year post-doctoral medical fellowship or post-doctoral fellow and his full salary is paid by his home country, will his work experience count as a Canadian work experience under the EE-CEC?
Kind regards,
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question: If a foreign national holds an LMIA exempt work permit for a one-year post-doctoral medical fellowship or post-doctoral fellow and his full salary is paid by his home country, will his work experience count as a Canadian work experience under the EE-CEC?
Answer:
A foreign national who holds a work permit under LMIA-exemption code C45 for a one-year post-doctoral medical fellowship is considered to be working. Under the International Mobility Program which covers C45, the foreign national is part of the Canadian labour force despite the lack of a Labour Market Impact Assessment.
Work is defined in Section 73(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Regulations: Despite the definition work in section 2, for the purposes of this Division, work means an activity for which wages are paid or commission is earned.
While a fellowship may be considered work for the purposes of their work permit, please note that if they are receiving a stipend or allowance, where the primary purpose is to cover expenses, this would not generally be considered wages (and therefore the work would not count for permanent residence). The onus is on the applicant to satisfy the officer that there was the payment of wages.
If all requirements are met, then the activity would count as qualifying Canadian work experience for the purposes of applying for permanent residence.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: DLI non-credit programming and study-permit holders -- REP-2021-0335
threads.question:
Good day,
Study permit holders who enrol in a non-credit program at a DLl would be considered for non-compliance in regards to study permit conditions, as non-credit programs with the exception of ESL are not considered as an active pursue of study.
Although the school is a DLl, and is now accepting study-permit holders from non-credit programming, these non-credit courses are not considered as "studies" as per R188(1)(c). Consequently, IRCC would not consider these students as enrolled and actively pursuing studies.
As for PGWP eligibilities, please note a study permit holder who enrol in a non-credit program before enrolling in a PGWP-eligible program may impact their PGWP eligibility because of non-compliance of the study permit condition.
For more information on PGWP eligibilities please visit our website.
I hope that this information is helpful to you

threads.subject: EE CRS and FSW-Professional degree needed to practice in a licensed profession -- REP-2020-2812
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
My name is I am an RCIC I have a prospective client whose primary occupation is NOC 3234 — Paramedical occupations Skill Level B and whose foreign education is equivalent to the Canadian First professional degree in medicine. Could you please direct me with
regards to the following:
1) Do you accept ECA performed by MCC for applicants whose primary occupation is not NOC 3111 or NOC 3112? The IRCC website specifies that applicants under NOC 3111 or NOC 3112 must complete an ECA with Medical Council of Canada (MCC), however there is no explicit prohibition that applicants under other medical occupations cannot use MCC as an education assessment provider.
2)EE CRS: In this situation, will the person be awarded CRS points for “Master's degree, OR professional degree needed to practice in a licensed profession"? As per this IRCC web page tool, First professional degree in medicine is equivalent to Professional degree needed to practice in a licensed profession and is awarded 135 points (without a spouse). However, according to Ministerial Instructions respecting Express Entry, those points are awarded for education "the level of an entry-to-practice professional degree for an occupation listed in the National Occupational Classification matrix at Skill level A for which licensing by a provincial regulatory body is required" while the primary NOC of the person (NOC 3234) is in Skill Level B.
3) If the person doesn't qualify for 135 points as described above, how many points will they be awarded under CRS and which level of education, if not the "level of entry-to practice", shall we indicate in the EE profile?
4) How many points will the applicant be awarded under the Federal Skilled Worker score grid for education factor?
Thank you in advance for your clarifications.
Sincerely,
RCIC
Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant
Answer:
If the degree is considered an international medical degree than an ECA from MCC may be accepted. The Medical Council of Canada (MCC) is an ECA service provider organization –providing Educational Credential Assessments for immigration purposes (to IRCC), as well as for other credential recognition uses in the field of medicine. I'd invite you to visit MCC's ECAlanding page on their website, where they outline that they are able to provide
assessments only for International Medical Graduates (IMGs) for immigration purposes. As mentioned by IRCC website you pointed to, the occupations are those that fit the NOC 3111 or NOC 3112 definitions.
In order to be considered under “First professional degree or entry-to-practice professional degree" by IRCC (and to be awarded points accordingly), the occupation must be categorized as a Skill Level A occupation and one of the eight occupations currently considered under the definition – which are medicine, veterinary medicine, dentistry, podiatry, optometry and law. Once received, the ECAreport will identify the education credential awarded.
To determine points under the Federal Skilled Worker score grid for education factor please see the following IRCC web page tool as it outlines the equivalency outcomes under both CRS and FSWP factor points. Points will be awarded in accordance with 78(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR).
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Who can't work off campus
You can't work off campus without a work permit if any of these situations apply to you:
Cioyenneté Canada
- your study permit says you aren't authorized to work off campus while you study
- you’re only enrolled in an English or French as a second language (ESL/FSL) program
- you're only taking general interest courses
- you're only taking courses required to be accepted into a full-time program
- your situation changes and you no longer meet all of the requirements to work off campus
If any ofthese situations apply to you, and you want to work while studying in Canada, you need to apply for a work permit
If your study situation changes
If you weren't eligible to work off campus, but your study situation has now changed, you may be able to change the conditions of your study permit.
You can apply to change the conditions of your permit if:
- you've changed your study program to one that may allow you to work off campus and
- your study permit says “This permit does not permit the holder to engage in off campus employment in Canada”
OR
- we included a condition on your study permit that may no longer apply
Example: You have a study permit to complete prerequisite courses, such as an ESL or FSL course. You’re then accepted into a full-time study program. This would mean you could apply to have the condition (not being allowed to work off campus) removed from your study permit.
You must apply to change the conditions of your study permit. There’s a fee to make this change. You must change the conditions on your permit before you can apply for a SIN.
Changing the conditions on your study permit
You'll need to apply for a new study permit from within Canada.

There may be two employers associated to the CRA business number (far instance, Mr. and Mrs. Smith, for that one full-time employment).
If an applicant is approved under that job offer, they would need to be mindful that their acceptance under the pilot was based on the information in that job offer (e.g., work description, details about the individuals requiring care, hours of work, wages, etc.). As such, an applicant approved under the pilot should carefully consider the risk in changing employers, particularly if the new work arrangement that differs substantially from the initial job offer. For exmple, accumulating part-time employment for multiple employers to make 30 hours of work in a week may or may not be considered by an officer to be equivalent to 30 hours ofeligible full-time care, as the part-time do not appear consistent with the full-time care needs of the person receiving care.
The occupation-restricted open work permit is a program design feature that is provided, in place of an employer-specified work permit, in order to facilitate the change of employers when required (for instance, if an employer terminated employment, or does not meet obligations towards the employee, or is abusive). It was not intended to be used to seekalternative forms of employment in those occupations (for instance, in institutional caregiving situations, or placement-agency based part-time work, where care needs are generally different and travel time may be included in the hours of work). This is because the programs are in place to meet a specific labour market need (the full-time in-home caregiving needs of Canadian families).

threads.answer:

Question: International companies are hiring Canadian consulting firms so that their previous or current clients can come to Canada and be hired by the Canadian company to continue to consult with the employee's previous employer. So the
previous employment becomes a "client".
The Canadian company is a legitimate Canadian limited company with physical locations and staff. They pay the employee's wage including deductions. They also issue the employee's T4. However it is arguable that they do not really issue instructions to the employee nor do they have the ability to fire the employee due to performance and they do not review the employee's productivity as the international client is responsible for doing so. Although the pay structure suggests that it is Canadian employment it is not an employee vs employer relationship which I would assume would make it illegitimate employment in regards to CEC. I would sincerely appreciate more clarification on the above if possible.
Answer: The onus is on the applicant to provide supporting documents and satisfy the officer that they meet all program requirements under the CEC and prove they are not self-employed. The CEC requires that applicants demonstrate they acquired skilled work experience in Canada through authorized employment by a third party. For your information, our internal guidance to determine whether an applicant under CEC was an employee or a self-employed individual during their period of qualifying work experience can be found on our website. Please note that each application under the CEC will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. (Note: If the prospective applicant is not sure of their employment status, they may choose to request a ruling from the CRA to have their status determined. Such a ruling will state whether, in the view of the CRA, a worker is an employee or self-employed. The link provided also contains indicators which show whether someone is an employee or self-employed. It should be noted that individuals who hold substantial ownership and/or exercise management control of a business for which they are also employed are generally considered to be self-employed. While the CRA ruling on an applicant's employment status will be given due consideration, such a ruling will not constitute conclusive evidence. The final decision as to the employment status of the applicant for the purposes of meeting CEC requirements rests with the Officer.) We trust that this information will assist you.

threads.subject: Postdocs holding Postdoc Association Positions -- REP-2021-0456
threads.question:
# Hello,
My name is, and I am a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant employed at the I am hoping you can provide us an official opinion on the following, which was recently brought up to us from the
There are 6 executive team positions available on the PDAC, and each executive is elected into the position for a 12month term, and receives an honorarium of $350 per month.
The question that has been brought up to us, is that there is a large international postdoctoral population here at the a majority of which are in possession of C44-LMIA exempt employer specific work permits. In the event that an international postdoctoral associate gets elected onto the executive team, are they legally allowed to perform the executive duties, and receive the honorarium, on their work permits? Being as these are elected positions, and only current postdocs are eligible to run, the honorarium and additional duties would not have been included on the employer portal submission for the work permits.
Please note the additional following details that were provided to us from the PDAC:
1. The PDAC Executive Team is composed of 6 positions
2. All individuals who fill the Executive Team positions must be current postdocs at the
3. Each position receives an honorarium of $350 per month, equating to $4,200 per annual term
4. The term of each position is 12 months, every position goes through another election after the year
5. There is no minimum time commitment required of the PDAC executive team positions. Each elected position dedicates to the PDAC the time that their postdoctoral position permits. On average, most positions commit around 1- 2hrs/week.
Based on the above, can you please provide us with an IRCC opinion to the question: In the event that an international postdoctoral associate gets elected onto the executive team, are they legally allowed to perform the executive duties, and
receive the honorarium, on their C-44 LMIA-exempt employer specific work permits?
We appreciate any guidance you're able to provide. Please let m know if you need any further information.
Kind regards,
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Hello,
QuESTioN: In the event that an international postdoctoral associate gets elected onto the executive team, are they legally allowed to perform the executive duties, and receive the honorarium, on their work permits? Being as these are elected positions, and only current postdocs are eligible to run, the honorarium and additional duties would not have been included on the employer portal submission for the work permits.
RESPoNSE: The Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations require that the employer provide the foreign worker with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as, but not less favourable than, those in the same offer [R209.2(1)(a)(iii)]. In this situation, assuming that the foreign worker must agree to be nominated, the occupation and work duties would not be viewed as 'less favourable than' just the duties of the post-doctoral occupation. The employer could justify the variance in duties by stating that the foreign worker agreed to the nomination, received extra experience and an honorarium, so therefore the variance was not detrimental to the worker.
In the future, I would suggest that the employer could add a line to the offer of employment indicating 'may be elected to PDAC Executive Team' which would cover them for any future offers of employment.
For more information on 'Variance in duties' and how IRCC assesses them you can review the officer guidance publically available here: Assessing compliance conditions. Specifically, the section titled : Occupation, wages and working conditions

Réponse : Les personnes qui présentent une demande de résidence permanente au Canada doivent mentionner les noms des membres de leur famille dans leur demande. Tous les membres de la famille doivent également faire l’objet d’un contrôle dans le cadre de la demande de résidence permanente afin de s’assurer qu’il n’existe aucune interdiction de territoire rendant le demandeur principal inadmissible à la résidence permanente, que les membres de sa famille l’accompagnent au Canada ou non. Cela vise les personnes suivantes : son époux/épouse ou conjoint(e) de fait, ses enfants à charge, les enfants à charge de son époux/épouse ou conjoint(e) de fait et les enfants à charge d’enfants à charge.
Si le/la conjoint(e) de fait est interdit(e) de territoire, la demande de résidence permanente pourrait également être refusée en raison de l’interdiction de territoire d’un membre de la famille même si celui--ci n’accompagne pas le demandeur principal, en vertu de l’article 42 de la Loi sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés (LiPR)/l’article 23 du Règlement sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés (RiPR). On recommande au/à la conjoint(e) de fait du demandeur principal, avant que ce dernier ne présente une demande de résidence permanente, de prendre des mesures afin de remédier à son interdiction de territoire.
En vertu de l’article 42 de la LiPR, une personne à qui l’on a accordé la résidence temporaire au Canada n’est pas interdite de territoire si son/sa conjoint(e) de fait est interdit(e) de territoire (pour des motifs autres que ceux mentionnés aux articles 34, 35 ou 37). Bien qu’un agent qui examine la demande de résidence permanente puisse déterminer que le demandeur principal n’est pas admissible à la résidence permanente au titre de l’article 42 de la LiPR et de l’article 23 du RIPR en raison du/de la conjoint(e) de fait interdit(e) de territoire qui l’accompagne, le demandeur principal ne perdrait pas son statut de résident temporaire au Canada.

documentation suffisante pour convaincre un agent qu’il satisfait aux exigences.

threads.question:
Dear IMMREP Officer,
I have a question with respect to CRS points for Express Entry for Intra-company transfer work permit holder.
A Foreign National (FN) has obtained an Intra-Company Transfer Work Permit under 205(a) (C-12) as a Managing Director (NOC 0). The Canadian corporation is wholly owned by a foreign corporate entity. The FN is the majority shareholder of that foreign corporation. The FN national is currently employed by the Canadian corporation as a Managing Director and is on their payroll.
For the purposes of applying for permanent residency under Express Entry in either CEC or FSW category:
1) Is the FN considered to be engaged in 'self-employment' or 'Self-employed'? (what definition of self-employment is used?)
2) After one year of Canadian work experience, is the FN eligible for the 200 CRS points for a qualifying offer of arranged employment? (per. 29(2)(a)(iïi Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Express Entry System )
3) After acquiring one year of Canadian work experience and subject to attaining sufficient CRS points to obtain ITA, is the FN eligible to apply under either Federal Skilled Working class or Canadian Experience Class?
Thanks,
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: A Foreign National (FN) has obtained an Intra-Company Transfer Work Permit under 205(a) (C-12) as a Managing Director (NOC 0). The Canadian corporation is wholly owned by a foreign corporate entity. The FN is the majority shareholder of that foreign corporation. The FN national is currently employed by the Canadian corporation as a Managing Director and is on their payroll. For the purposes of applying for permanent residency under Express Entry in either CEC or FSW category: Is the FN considered to be engaged in 'self-employment' or 'Self-employed'? (what definition of self-employment is used?)
Answer: Program requirements vary between Express Entry programs. For the Canadian Experience Class, the onus is on the applicant to provide supporting documents and satisfy the officer that they meet all program requirements and prove they are not self-employed. The CEC requires that applicants demonstrate they acquired skilled work experience in Canada through authorized employment by a third party. For your information, our internal guidance to determine whether an applicant under CEC was an employee or a self-employed individual during their period of qualifying work experience can be found on our website. Please note that each application under the CEC will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. For the Federal Skilled Worker program, there is no such restrictions on self-employment, but applicants must continue to meet all program requirements, as per section 75 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
Note: If the prospective applicant is not sure of their employment status, they may choose to request a ruling from the
CRA to have their status determined. Such a ruling will state whether, in the view of the CRA, a worker is an employee or self-employed. The link provided also contains indicators which show whether someone is an employee or self-employed. It should be noted that individuals who hold substantial ownership and/or exercise management control of a business for which they are also employed are generally considered to be self-employed. While the CRA ruling on an applicant's employment status will be given due consideration, such a ruling will not constitute conclusive evidence. The final decision as to the employment status of the applicant rests with the Officer. Question: After one year of Canadian work experience, is the FN eligible for the 200 CRS points for a qualifying offer of arranged employment? (per. 29(2)(a)(ii) Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Express Entry System ) Answer: The Express Entry applicant can obtain CRS points for a qualifying offer of arranged employment, so long as they meet the requirements as defined under section 29 of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system.
Question: After acquiring one year of Canadian work experience and subject to attaining sufficient CRS points to obtain ITA, is the FN eligible to apply under either Federal Skilled Working class or Canadian Experience Class?
Answer: Please note that we do not provide case-specific guidance. The applicant should apply for the program in which they meet the eligibility requirements and can provide sufficient supporting documentation upon application.
and Cizenship Canedaot Cioyenneté Canada
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

- is employed in an occupation that falls within National Occupational Classification (NOC) skill type 0 (management occupations) or skill level A or B (which generally includes professional occupations and technical or skilled trades [see the NOC website]);
- physically resides or plans to physically reside in Canada while working.
My question is trying to clarify if there is a hierarchical approach to determining eligibility (General conditions must be met, plus any specific conditions listed, in order to be eligible OR specific eligibility requirements alone satisfy eligibility).
Answer: Under the International Mobility Program (IMP), a dependent spouse or common law partner is eligible to apply for an open work permit under LMIA exemption code C41 if the principal foreign worker meets all of the eligibility requirements listed on our website. The policy then lists the specific eligibility requirements based on the type of work permit the principal applicant has (bridging open work permit, open work permit) or specific work permit program the principal applicant holds a work permit under. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet eligibility and admissibility requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

threads.subject: Police Certificates for Permanent Residence-Express Entry -- REP-2021-0612
threads.question:
From #
Dear Agent,
I refer to this link:
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/apply-permanent-residence/police-certificates.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/apply-permanent-residence/police-certificates.html)
There are 2 scenarios for assessing the validity of police certificates:
1. If you live in the country currently, then the police certificate must be issued within 6 months of filing the case -ie. within the last six months while you're still living there.
2. If you previously lived in the country, then the police certificate must be issued after the last time your stayed there for 6 months or more in a row. We need clarification on this.
a. Does this mean: that you have to have physically left the country in order to apply for the police certificate? That would be difficult as that no person could ever apply for a police certificate while physically in the country, even if they leave the country the week after.
b. Or, does this mean that IRCC applies the same logic as they do for the test for police certificates from your current country–that the police certificate must be issued within six months of leaving the country (so you that you're not in the country for 6 months or more without having had a police certificate). The way the 6 months is counted is that from the time you get your police certificate, you cannot remain in the country to trigger the police certificate requirement again. For example, if you obtain a police certificate in May 2017 from country X, then leave country X in August 2017–meaning you were in the country 3 months -you would not trigger a new police certificate requirement because you would not in the country for a new ‘six months in a row'.
This would then enable certain applicants to re-use the police certificate for permanent residence that applicants use to get their work permits, as long as the applicant left their country within 6 months of issuance of the police certificate.
Your assistance is greatly appreciated. Thank you.
Kind regards,
Page 3113
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
L'information divulguée en vertu de la toi sur Faccés à Tinfomation
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's (IRCC) Immigration Representatives mailbox.
In response to your first question, you are correct. Applicants are requested to submit a police certificate for countries they have resided for more than 6 months since the age of 18 along with their application for permanent residence. Furthermore, applicants may request a police certificate while living in their current country of residence, as long as they are still residing in this country at the time of submitting their application.
This being said, police certificate requirements may vary according to each line of business. We recommend reviewing the specific requirements for each line of business, as you have done so for Police certificates for Express Entry applications-Canada.ca. As you may have noticed, Express Entry requirements state that the police certificate for the country where you currently live must be issued no more than 6 months before the date you submit your application and must not be expired.
Also of note for Express Entry applications, if your client is invited to apply, they have 90 days to submit their application for permanent residence. If they do not have all their police certificates by the 90-day deadline, they have 2 options:
Option 1: Decline your invitation to apply
Their profile will go back in the pool and they may be invited to apply again.
Option 2: Prove you applied for the police certificate In very rare cases, IRCC may accept both a letter of explanation and proof that shows your client made your best effort to get a police certificate on time.
With regard to your question 2(b), it would appear that your client's police certificate does not cover the entire period (more than six months in a row until August 2017) they resided in country X. We suggest requesting a new police certificate from the country's authorities which covers the period your client resided in country X for more than 6 months in a row, thus until August 2017.
As with any case, the officer reviewing the file may require further documentation in order to be satisfied that the applicant is not criminally inadmissible.
We trust that this information will be useful to you.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: (URGENT) Important Deficiency in French TR to RP Pathway Portal for International Graduates-Misleading -- REP-2021-0771
threads.question:
Good day,
I assisted clients to present PR applications under the TR to PR Pathway, under the French Speaking International Graduates Stram (Diplômés étrangers d’expression française).
It has been reported by my clients that under the portal, there is a very important mistake, which induced many people in error:
In fact, on the French version of the Portal, there is no Proof of education Field. Instead, it has been replaced by a “Expérience de travail qualifié" field, even though international graduates don't have to proof qualified work experience under a specific NOC
Cioyenneté Canada
code under this stream; they only have to prove they are employed.
Only in the English version of the form will people find a “Proof of Education field”.
This has lead to many issues. Clients who uploaded the forms following the French version of the online portal checklist got misleaded and did not, in many instances, submit their educationl credentials as there was no field for that purposes. They thought that they would have to submit other employment evidence. Many clients are panicking as they are scared of seeing their application rejected and not being able to send their proof of education documents to IRCC,
Although, in the English version, there is a proof of education field. It appears that a clear mistake was commited when building the French version of the portal.
The French version of the portal should have a Proof of education” field, especially considering that this portal is designed to be a DIY and representatives are not allowed to upload documents for their clients.
In that sense, we plead IRCC to not outright reject applications under this stream, considering these facts. There are not many applicants under this stream.
Please permit applicants to submit their academical credentials via webform or through any other viable mean, in respect of procedural fairness and in consideration that the form contains a clear mistake.
Would you please confirm that said issue will be resolved and that the French version of the TR to RP portal will have a Proof of education field as to not mislead applicants anymore?

Best regards,
Citoyenneté Canada

threads.question:
Hi there,
Hope all is well. I need to clarify the minimum requirements under CEC.
- have at least 1 year of skilled work experience in Canada, in the last 3 years before you apply
If the candidate is not currently working, Does the 3-year time frame start from the date ofITA or the date of AOR?
For example. Received ITA on January 1, 2021 and submitted eAPR on March 1, 2021.

threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: I need to clarify the minimum requirements under CEC." Have at least 1 year of skilled work experience in Canada, in the last 3 years before you apply." If the candidate is not currently working, does the 3-year time frame start from the date of ITA or the date of AOR? For example. Received ITA on January 1, 2021 and submitted e-APR on March 1, 2021. 3 years' time frame: January 1, 2018 ~ January 1, 2021 or March 1, 2018 ~ March 1, 2021??
Answer: For the Canadian Experience Class (CEC), applicants must have acquired in Canada, within the three years before the date on which their application for permanent residence (e-APR) is made, at least one year of full-time work experience, or the equivalent in part-time work experience, as per R87.1(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. threads.subject: Clarification-Location of work for C16 work permit holders -- REP-2021-0654
threads.question:
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Hi there,
I am seeking clarification on the LMIA-exempt code C16 - Francophone Mobility. This program has been created to favor the immigration of francophone workers outside of Quebec (QC). Would you be able to confirm if my interpretation of the following scenarios is correct: Company in QC, foreigner working from any other province than QC --> eligible to C16 Company in any other province than QC, foreigner working from QC --> not eligible to C16 I am basically seeking confirmation that what matters is where the foreign worker physically resides and works from, regardless of where the company's office is located. Thanks for your help with this,
threads.answer:
Dear
The policy intent of this exemption is to encourage the development of minority official language communities in Canada. Promoting the use of French outside Quebec strengthens and supports the social and cultural fabric of Canadian society, while respecting the federal, bilingual and multicultural character of Canada. While it is not prohibited to conduct some professional activities in Quebec, the FN should work most of the time outside of Quebec. For example, it would be against the policy intent to telework from, or work in Quebec on a regular basis.
The examples stated below may be acceptable as long as they are incidental/exceptional to the FN main duties and are unanticipated, temporary, or limited in nature., but this would depend on the case specifics.
a. The FN is based outside of Quebec but needs to attend a conference in Quebec.
b. The FN is based outside of Quebec but from time to time has to visit Quebec based customers of the employer for business meetings.
c. The FN is based outside of Quebec but from time to time has to visit Quebec based customers of the employer to provide on-site professional consulting services.
d. The FN is based outside of Quebec but from time to time attends at the employer's premises in Montreal to undertake his or her duties there (for example, a manager from outside Quebec who visits an office in Quebec for a couple of days every 6 weeks for to meet with personnel there)

Question: For a Canadian Experience Class via Express Entry application, when an applicant with arranged employment, is there an obligation for that person to keep an employer-specific work permit right through to the end of processing the permanent resident application or would that person continue to qualify for arranged employment after receiving a Bridging Open Work Permit?
Answer: Under Canadian Experience Class, applicants do not have to be employed at the time of application, but must have temporary status during the qualifying period of work experience acquired in Canada, as per R87.1(3)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. Candidates are responsible for ensuring that the information in their profile is up-to- date at all times, so any changes in circumstance (including a BOWP) should be communicated via their profile. For the applicant to be eligible for arranged employment points, they must continue to meet the criteria as defined under section
29(2) of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Break in studies -- REP-2021-0764
threads.question:
hi IRCC,
1. If an international student fails in their first semester of college and within 150 days they get enrolled in a different college and course and inform IRCC through the mycic portal by flling out Change of DLI information, are they good to go? Can they resume working part time?
2. They will need an additional 5 months of Study Permit that needs to be extended, can they apply for study permit extension when they are closer to the expiration date of the current Study Permit or should they apply for the study permit right now? (Student is still left with about 14 months of study permit. )
threads.answer:
Hello
Thank you for your inquiry. Kindly see the responses below.
1. Students engaging in post-secondary studies in Canada may transfer between institutions (both public and private) or change their course or program of study without applying for a change to the condition of their study permit, as long as the receiving institution is a DLI. Students should notify IRCC through their MyAccount when they transfer to another DLI. Students who transfer DLls may resume working in Canada as long as they meet all the on-campus and off-campus work eligibility requirements.
2. Students who want to extend their study permit to keep studying must apply to extend their permit at least 30 days before it expires.

threads.question:
Dear Sir/ Madam,
My question is the following: Is the spouse of an international student who is studying Language for 2 school terms and later will attend a one year post-graduate certificate program eligible for work during the language studies?
Thanks & regards,
and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Hello,
If the spouse is studying at a DLl and has obtained a study permit for the duration of their language studies, they may be eligible to work, provided they meet all the conditions of their study permit. In general, this means they can work up to 20 hours per week off-campus during their studies without needing a work permit.
If the language studies are being completed at a non-designated leaning institution, the spouse would be unable to obtain a study permit and therefore, would be unable to work during this portion of their studies.

threads.question:
Bonjour,
Les étudiants qui se trouvent déjà au Canada et qui ont demandé un permis de travail – stage coop peuvent commencer leur stage coop grâce à leur autorisation du programme à travailler sur le campus et hors campus, à condition de respecter tous les critères d’admissibilité.
Les étudiants peuvent travailler à temps plein sur le campus de l’université ou du collège qu’ils fréquentent à temps plein conformément au [R186f)]. Dans le cadre de l’autorisation du programme de travail hors campus [R186v)], ils peuvent travailler jusqu’à 20 heures par semaine pendant un trimestre ou un semestre d’études, ce qui comprend à la fois les heures prévues au stage coop et les heures consacrées à leur emploi rémunéré normal (s’ils en ont un). Ils peuvent également travailler à temps plein pendant les congés prévus au calendrier d’études.
Toutefois, si la demande de stage coop est refusée, l’étudiant doit cesser de travailler immédiatement.
Si vous avez d’autres questions, n’hésitez pas à nous recontacter.
Cordialement,
Représentants immigration (IRCC)

spousal OWP extension IMM5710).
Response to Scenario: Please note that this service is to give general functional guidance, thus we are not able to provide case-specific advice. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements. For case-specific resources and assistance, see the links below.
Question #1: If visitor extension is granted before the WP is processed, will the WP application be treated as an application to extend that visitor status and granted?
Answer #1: If the FN submits form IMM5708, the application to change conditions, extend stay or remain in Canada as a visitor and this change is approved, the OWP application will be processed under their current status. The approval of form IMM5708 does not guarantee the approval of the work permit.
Question #2: If visitor extension is not granted before the WP is processed, will the WP be processed as priority instead of the visitor extension?
Answer #2: The WP will not be processed as priority if the visitor extension is not granted as this circumstance does not fall under one of the streams for priority processing.
Question #3: What, if anything, should the applicant do to alert IRCC to the two interplaying applications, given that
ultimately what the FN wants is to get a spousal OWP?
Answer #3: The applicant does not need to take additional steps to alert IRCC of the two applications.

threads.question:
Hello,
If the temporary foreign worker falls within one of the exempted occupations (such as 0821-Agricultural Managers), they are exempted from the Mandatory Hotel Stay. In that case, the worker needs to have no symptoms of COVID-19, has to travel to the final place of quarantine in a private vehicle and has to travel only with those who arrived on the same flight. If all these criteria are met, then the temporary foreign worker is exempted from the Mandatory Hotel Stay. For more information visit this website.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Postdoctoral fellow and visiting professor-Canadian Work Experience -- REP-2021-0437
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to ’s Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
My questions are:
1- Does time spent in Canada as a visiting scholar or professor count towards Canadian work experience for Express Entry? This was time spent working in Canada with a temporary work permit, but the person is paid by home university.
2- Does time spent in Canada as a postdoctoral fellow count towards Canadian work experience for Express Entry? This was time spent working in Canada with a temporary work permit, and the person is paid by the Canadian university.
3- Given that a postdoctoral fellow has been offered a contract extension to the second year, is it considered a valid job offer for Express Entry that is worth 50 CRS points?
Answer:
1- Please note that we do not respond to case specific questions. Based on the information provided however, this experience may constitute Canadian work experience. To apply for permanent residence under the Canadian Experience Class, your skilled work experience must:
- be in a job classified as skill type 0, or skill level A or B according to the 2016 National Occupational Classification,
- amount to at least one year of full-time (or an equal amount in part-time) in the previous three years,
- have been with an employer in Canada (self-employment does not count),
- be gained with the proper legal authorization (for example, as a documented worker with a valid work permit), and
- not be gained while you were studying on a student permit.
The experience you describe as a fellow in Canada on a temporary work permit may be counted as work experience, and not study, provided it meets the definition of work pursuant to Section 73(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, which states: despite the definition work in section 2, for the purposes of this Division, work means an activity for which wages are paid or commission is earned. Please note that to be considered work, the applicant must have been paid wages or commission. A stipend or allowance, where the primary purpose is to cover expenses, would not generally be considered wages. The onus is on the applicant to satisfy the officer that there was the payment of wages and that all other requirements were met.
2- The experience you describe as a fellow in Canada on a temporary work permit may be counted as work experience, and not study, provided it meets the definition of work pursuant to Section 73(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, which states: despite the definition of work in section 2, for the purposes of this Division, work means an activity for which wages are paid or commission is earned. Please note that to be considered work, the application must have been paid wages or commission. A stipend or allowance, where the primary purpose is to cover expenses, would not generally be considered wages. The onus is on the applicant to satisfy the officer that there was a payment of wages and that all other requirements were met. 3- Your job offer must:
- be recent (usually less than 1 year old) (You can't use the same job offer letter that you used to get your work permit.)
- be in writing
- not be from an embassy, high commission or consulate in Canada
- set out details of the job they're offering you, such as
- your pay and deductions
- your job duties conditions of employment, like your hours of work

threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
I was hoping to receive some clarity regarding the comprehensive ranking system under Express Entry and the eligibility for applicants to receive the additional points for the completion of Canadian education (the 15 or 30 points).
Due to COVID-19, many students have started their Canadian education from outside Canada and waiting for the approvals of their study permit to be able to enter Canada, some student may not be able to enter Canada to complete at least 8 months of their program in Canada to be eligible for the additional education points-will there be exceptions made for these groups of students? For example, if a student entered Canada on January 15, 2021 and completed their program on August 31, 2021 (just less than 8 months of physical presence in Canada), will the student be eligible for the additional education points?
I also understand that distance learning for Canadian programs count towards education points, but not for the additional education points — will an exceptions be made due to COVID-19 and programs (which were supposed to be in-person programs) being switched to online-only format? For example, if a student was in Canada for a one year Master's program that started in September 2020 and was forced to study online for the entirety of their program due to COVID-19 (Fall 2020, Winter 2021 and Spring 2021), although the student is physically in Canada, will they be granted the additional points for education?
Answer:
For Express Entry, there have been no changes to the Ministerial Instructions with respect to online learning or studying outside of Canada. A Canadian educational credential cannot be awarded if the credentials were obtained in a study or training program in which distance learning amounted to more than half of the program length.
Pursuant to R73.1, a Canadian educational credential means any diploma, certificate or credential, issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions. In addition, the credential must meet the requirements stated in the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions – MI 1 1(3) and MI 30 (1)-(5). Please see below:
Educational credentials

Exceptions

- (a) credentials obtained in a study or training program in which the study of English or French as a second language amounted to more than half of the program;

threads.answer: 0557) -- REP-2021-0651 Good day, Thank you for your enquiry. In circumstances where a client is eligible to apply for a TRV from within Canada but has left the country before receiving their counterfoil, they may submit a web form to request that they be able to send their passport to a visa office outside of Canada to have the counterfoil affixed. For common-law partner sponsorship applications, it is possible for the sponsor to meet the eligibility criteria (sponsorship eligibility passed) and the PR application to not meet the eligibility criteria (PA eligibility not passed) if the sponsor is a Canadian PR who did not declare the sponsored person as common-law on their PR application and indicated they were single.
As per R130, a sponsor must be 18 years of age or older; be a Canadian citizen or permanent resident; reside in Canada if a Permanent Resident (If Canadian citizen, they intend to return) file a sponsorship application in respect of a member of the family class in accordance with section 10; and if the sponsor landed as the Principal Applicant (PA) under the FC1, FCC or FCE categories, 5 years must elapse since the date of landing before they are eligiblè to sponsor a new spouse, common-law partner or conjugal partner. With respect to R130(1) (c ) verify that the sponsor does not have an existing FC1, FCC or FCE undertaking at the time of lock-in. There can be no new sponsorship if there is an existing sponsorship undertaking in respect of a spouse, common-law partner or conjugal partner and the three-year period of that sponsorship has not ended. Although not outlined in R130, a Registered Indian can also be a sponsor.
A sponsor is barred from sponsorship under R133(1)(a) if they are not a “sponsor" as per Immigration legislation. This occurs when a sponsor does not meet the definition of a sponsor under R130, including when the PA is not a member of the Family Class. If the sponsored person was not declared and/or examined, the possibility of exclusion under R117(9)(d) exists. Exclusions under R117(9)(d) are examined and a determination made at the visa office on a case by case basis.
Applicants for permanent residence are obligated to divulge the existence of all of their dependants to the processing office on their application forms, and for most immigration categories to have these dependants examined. Or, if a dependant is acquired through marriage, birth or adoption prior to landing, the sponsor is obligated to inform the visa post of this new dependant. When an applicant arrives at a port of entry with their IMM1000 or COPR they are asked at landing if they have any other dependants not listed on the document. The applicant must divulge the existence of a dependant not declared to the visa post at the port of entry. Sponsors who are not Canadian Citizens and sponsors who were not landed CR may be reportable under 44(1) for failure to declare dependants, which could render the sponsor inadmissible to Canada.

Kindly note that students are considered to be meeting the conditions of their study permit as long as they are enrolled in a DLl, and they are actively pursuing their studies (i.e., they can demonstrate that they are making reasonable progress towards the completion of their courses in the time allotted), whether the program is credited or non-credited.
Students who take non-credited courses before enrolling in a credited certificate, diploma or degree program which meets the PGWPP eligibility criteria, should not be impacted in regards to the PGWPP as long as they meet all the other PGWPP eligibility criteria during their enrolment in the credited certificate, diploma or degree. However, the length of the PGWP will only be based on the eligible program.
It should also be noted that in order to work off-campus under R186(v), students must be full-time and enrolled in a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program, or a vocational training program at the secondary level offered in Quebec of 6 months or longer that leads to a degree, diploma, degree or certificate. Therefore, part-time or full-time students enrolled in only in non-credited courses are not eligible to work off-campus.

If the student does not meet the below eligibility reguirements, they will not be eligible to apply for a PGWP.
To obtain a post-graduation work permit, the applicant must currently hold valid temporary status or have left Canada. They must have graduated from an eligible designated learning institution (DLl). Exceptions can be made only for the following: 0 leave from studies 0 final academic session They have received a transcript and an official letter from the eligible DLl confirming that they have met the requirements to complete their program of study.
Please be advised that any leave taken from a program of studies in Canada should not exceed 150 days from the date the leave commenced and must be authorized by their DLI.
The student can work full-time until we make a decision on their PGWP if:
had a valid study permit when they submitted their application,
•completed their study program, AND
were eligible to work off campus without a work permit while studying and they didn't work more hours than they
were allowed to.

If these conditions don't apply, the student must wait until their work permit arrives to begin working. It's illegal to work in Canada without authorization.

threads.question:
Hello,
Question: Can a placement agency be the employer under an LMIA application? In the province of Quebec its forbidden. Is it allowed under the immigration act? A placement agency, meaning rents an employee to another Canadian employer.
Response: In general, companies cannot bring in workers who are not directly working for them. A business cannot hire foreign nationals and place them in third party locations. They can only hire and bring in workers who will directly employed by them. For information on the responsibilities for an offer of employment, you may review the instructions and information found in the Employer Portal enrollment guide for information on 'Who needs to complete an offer of employment.' If there was an instance where two Canadian companies are involved in the process of hiring a temporary foreign worker, the employer of record will be the one to submit to the offer of employer. The employer of record is the company that will ensure both employers are following the conditions of employing a temporary foreign worker. Find out more about these conditions and your responsibilities as an employer. In all cases, the employer of record must be involved in hiring the temporary worker. This can include setting up the details of the job they wil do and overseeing their work. For more information and case-specific guidance, please see the resources below.

The IRCC website's Q&A section mentions specifically that the spouse being sponsored must be 18 years old when IRCC receives the application (not when the couple is married). I have enclosed a copy of the section to my email for easy access.

mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Due to the impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic on our operations, we have experienced delays in providing a response.
As per R117(9)(a) and R5(a), both spouses must be at least 18 years of age at the time of submitting their sponsorship application in order to be considered as a member of the family class. As long as it is legal to be married before the age of 18 in the country where the couple was married, then the couple would be allowed to submit their application once they both turn 18 years old.

Hello,
I hope you and your colleagues are well. I am writing with two questions on behalf of our students at :
We have many students who transfer to our institution from other post-secondary schools in Canada and I am hoping you can clarify how the scheduled break provisions for off-campus work under R186(v) would apply to these students in their transferring terms. The Summer term (May-August) is a scheduled break for our undergraduates; however, we do have many transfer students who choose to join us in Summer as well as in Fall.
- For students who are joining our institution in Summer (starting in May), can this term still be considered a scheduled break (allowing students to work full time regardless of their course load with us) provided they were enrolled full time in an eligible program at their previous institution in the term immediately prior, and assuming they will enroll full time at our institution in the term immediately following? Note that most of these students will not have completed a credential at their previous institution but instead are transferring their credits to be used toward their degree here. They may enroll on a part-time or full-time basis for the Summer term.
- For students who have been accepted to transfer to our institution in Fall (September) and will have a break between programs before starting with us, would these students be eligible to work full time in the Summer term provided they were enrolled full time in an eligible program at their previous institution in Winter/Spring (January-April) and will enroll full time with us in September? Again, these students will not have completed a credential at their previous
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
institution so they would not fall within the provision for students who have completed a program of study as outlined in the off-campus work PDIs (as they are not holding "written confirmation of program completion from their current institution").
We have received numerous questions regarding the above from our incoming transfer students, and while it seems logical that students who meet the requirement of full-time enrollment in an eligible program in the terms immediately before and after the break should be eligible for full-time work regardless of the change in institution/program, we would not want to put our students at risk of working without authorization if this interpretation is incorrect. Therefore, any clarification you are able to provide would be much appreciated.
Thanks in advance, and please feel free to let me know if you need any additional information or clarification regarding the above in order to respond.
Warm regards,
中 Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Hello Thank you for your inquiry.
Students may work full-time off-campus during a DLl's regularly scheduled break regardless of when they transfer to the new institution. In order to work off campus without a work permit under paragraph R186(v), students must hold full-time status during the academic session before and after their regularly scheduled break.
In order for a break to be considered a regularly scheduled break, the break must be part of the DLl's academic calendar (for instance, winter and summer holidays, Reading Week). Each regularly scheduled break should not be longer than 150 days. The maximum cumulative duration of scheduled breaks is 180 days per calendar year.
Thank you,

threads.question:
Dear Immigration Representatives,
I am an immigration lawyer working at a non-profit legal service in Edmonton. Can you please advise whether the Department would issue a Refugee Travel Document, to a protected person in Canada, that would be valid to return to the country of nationality (i.e., the country against which the refugee protection had been granted)? The reason for travel would be to pay the last visit to a terminally ill parent who is in no position to re-unite with the
protected person in a third country.

Yours truly,
and Cizenship Canadaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good Afternoon,
A Refugee Travel Document, which can be obtained from Passport Canada, is a document for people in Canada with protected-person status. It is recognized in all countries as a valid travel document; however, it cannot be used to travel to the country that the person is a citizen of or the country of claimed persecution. Further information can be found online: Refugee Travel Document requirements.
In addition, OP 16 / ENF 32 / IP 12 Passports and Travel Documents, section 7.10 Refugee Travel Document states "Refugee Travel Documents are issued by a competent authority of a country to persons recognized by that country as protected persons, pursuant to the 1951 UN Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, to facilitate the travel of the holder to other countries. The document prohibits travel to the country from which the holder fled persecution and allows the holder to return to the issuing country within the validity period of the document".
I hope this clarifies the issue.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
